speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CLAIM OF GOVERNMENT OF CANADA AGAINST UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
If the House wishes that I should
state the object of our visit and the result, I will do so. The object of the visit to Washington was to press the settlement of a claim that our government has against the government of the United States in reference to the seizure of certain properties seized by the Custodian of Alien Enemy Property of the United States. In 1918 and 1919 the Custodian of Alien Enemy Property of the United States government proceeded to seize certain certificates of shares and bonds of Canadian companies which were owned by enemies residing in Germany, which certificates' and bonds were then deposited with different institutions in the United States. Our own custodian, proceeding under our war measures act. had also seized some, if not all, of the same securities. Some of the companies which had been ordered by the American courts to pay their dividend to the Alien Property Custodian paid some of the dividends and then ceased to pay, on account of the vesting orders which had been issued by our
own courts. We tried to arrive at a settlement "a l'amiable." The Alien Property Custodian of the United States government came to Canada. The hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was then our custodian. I understand that he had some conferences with the representatives of the American government, and Mr. Mulvey was a party to the conferences. The question under discussion was whether we had any right in those securities, or whether they were to be left in possession of the American government. It was important that the dividends should be paid or deposited in the hands of one of the two governments. It was agreed that, pending the discussion, the dividends should be paid to the American government, and that the question of law should be decided by an arbitrator or by a judge of Canada or of the United States. Some of the Canadian companies continued to pay the dividends to the Alien Property Custodian of the United States. After a certain time that very question which was in doubt and discussed between the two governments was decided by the American court, at the request of the American officer, in reference to certain certificates of American companies which had been sequestered by the Alien Property Custodian of the Imperial government, and which certificates were deposited in England. The question was debated and decided in favour of the American government. Taking advantage of that decision, our attorneys tried to induce the American government to turn over to the Canadian government those certificates and bonds. Proceedings have been going on for gome years-since 1920. After consultation with our attorneys we were advised that it would be preferable that we should try and arrive at a settlement with the American government without litigation, and we were advised that if we had the opportunity of meeting the President of the United States, the Secretary of State and the Attorney General of that country, perhaps, after those three decisions-there were three decisions on that very same point'-the American gov -rnment would consent, without arbitration and without litigation, to hand over thos'e securities to our government. Accordingly our custodian, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Copp), Mr. Newcombe, Mr. Mulvey, and myself decided to go to Washington. Hon. Mr. Pugsley was not one of our party. We met the Secretary of State of the United States, who declared that he was perfectly willing to turn over to Canada th securities mentioned but thought the

Alien Enemy Property
President would be governed in the matter by the advice of the Attorney General, and that the only trouble in the way was the fact that after the orders had been rendered by the American courts, vesting those securities in the Alien Property Custodian of the United States, they did not see how that officer could take it upon himself to turn those properties over to Canada. We answered that we should invoke the three judgments which were rendered by the American courts at the request of the American authorities, and we did not see that there was any necessity of litigation any more, since the case had been decided in favour of the American government and, consequently, in our favour. The same objection was repeated that there was a distinction also, because registration had been made of those same stocks in favour of the American officer, and they were of opinion that it was necessary that a judgment should be rendered by some tribunal. We had the advantage of meeting the President and repeating the same argument. We were told that the American government were heartily disposed to liquidate the situation as promptly as possible, and that they would be willing to expedite any case that might be instituted by our government before any of the courts of the United States. We suggested that we would prefer to proceed before one of our courts as the American government did in proceeding before one of their judges. Later on, after those two interviews, a conference took place between the Assistant Attorney General and our representative, Mr. Conboy, and it was then agreed that to expedite matters, if we were to institute one or two cases in Canada, assigning one or two companies to appear before such court to be instructed to deliver to the Canadian government certificates for those same stocks, the American government would appear, so that the judgment would be binding upon the American government and upon the companies. This we found most, satisfactory.
As to the bonds, there may be some distinction to be made. Certificates of stocks are only evidence of property, while a bond is something by itself. We contended all the same that no distinction should be made. There is also the question of dividends which were paid to the American government. Our intention is to proceed, as I said, in one or two cases, to have the principle decided of the property in the stocks. If the judgment goes in our favour, necessarily we shall be entitled to dividends paid to the American government. As to the bonds, something

has to be done. We are now considering what is to be done, and when and how it should be done. On the whole we consider that we have accomplished something, and we hope that after a comparatively short delay, we shall get the securities to which we are entitled.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

I can prove conclusively that my statement was absolutely correct.

The hon. member for Lunenburg referred last night to an item of $96,122, reserve for doubtful debts and claims. That is an item on which we should have a little explanation. Has the Canadian Government. Merchant Marine been in the habit of running accounts or giving credit for goods transported? Is it unable to collect some os those accounts at the present time?

Supply-Merchant Marine

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend the item offhand; but, of course, in a business of this magnitude, there are some claims outstanding. I know in my own business, when I am making a statement, I set aside a certain amount for doubtful claims that may be paid hereafter or that may turn out to be worthless.

I have never known any transportation company, railway or steamship, to take any chances on cLaims for freight. 1 understood these were always collected before the goods were delivered and in many cases before the goods were received for transportation. I can hardly understand the Canadian Government Merchant Marine running monthly or weekly accounts for freight charges, if that is what this means.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: In many accounts for transportation, three or four different companies are interested because of interchange of freight, settlement of rates; and this is a reserve amount put aside to meet any of those settlements that might be unsatisfactory. This might not mean that the private individual had not paid his freight to some transportation company. .

I do not think there has been any other question asked as often in this House as the question: Why cannot the Canadian Government Merchant Marine be made to pay? This question has been repeated again; and again I might say that I was a little disappointed yesterday evening when the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) took his seat and, in my opinion, did not make even an attempt to explain the matter.
It is pretty hard to satisfy everybody.

I claim to have had ju*t a little experience in connection with steamboat work, and I have made the statement at least twice on the floor of this House that the smaller boats up to, say, 5,000 tons will never pay. I think it is incumbent upon me to explain that statement and show why, in my opinion, they will not pay. I am not criticizing the building of the boats; I am not criticizing the workmanship; nor am I criticizing the captains and the crews that operate these boats. But I do criticize the man who was responsible for the designing of them; I criticize the architect. I do not know who he is; I have never heard his name; but in my opinion it is evident that he never had any practical experience so far as freight boats are concerned. He may be a first-class architect from the standpoint of
passenger steamers, but freight boats are au entirely different proposition.
Let us consider the construction of some of these freight boats of 5,000 tons or less-I am referring to those that I have seen. They have a fair, clean run behind, but from the centre they taper off more in the fashion of passenger boats towards the bow. A freight boat should carry its beam well forward to the bow; the boats to which I am referring are less than five thousand tons and ought to have had anywhere from ten to fifteen feet more of a beam to give them carrying capacity. If that wrere the case they could carry at least a third more freight than they are able to take as they are, and it would not interfere with their speed to any extent. In a steamer that makes from eight to ten knots, it does not affect the speed to any appreciable extent to have a blunt bow, and this affords added carrying capacity. These boats are not built in that way; they are more like passenger boats. Then their engines and boilers are placed in the centre, which should not be. The engines should be placed in a freight boat as near the stem as it. is possible to get them. The boilers should be placed in the stem of the boat, taking up as little room as possible, just giving the firemen space enough in which to work. The firemen do not require more than room enough to enable them to attend to the boilers. In the bow of the boat there should be a bulkhead or watertight compartment, or tanks to hold water, so that when the boat is running light the tanks can be filled to prevent the ship from pounding in the sea. A boat in which the machinery is situated in the stern must have some ballast in the bow, because if she pounds in the sea she is bound to do herself material damage. These boats are not constructed in that manner. The centre of a freight boat of this size should be left entirely free for freight, but, as I have already pointed out, the machinery in these particular steamers is all in the centre. There should be two hatches instead of, as is the case with many of these boats, the whole decks covered with hatches. I think the architect sacrificed utility to beauty. Undoubtedly the boats do look well at sea; but that is not the main consideration in freight steamers. These boats should have carrying capacity, which is not provided in these particular steamers. As regards the boilers, any person who has had any practical experience in connection with machinery will admit that a boiler in a freight boat should have a lead anywhere from 25 to 35 per cent over the engines, for the simple reason that when inferior coal is being used the firemen
Supply-Merchant Marine

can still keep up steam. And, besides, it is much easier on the boiler. These boats have not got that feature; at least I have not seen it in any of those that I have looked over. I consider the boiler of a steamer the most important part of its equipment. When you have to force a boiler to keep up steam by forced draft, you are apt to have trouble with the combustion chamber, and the probability is that you will spring a leak. On getting into port with such boilers the first thing that has to be done is to draw fire and cool off the boiler, and it takes anywhere from 36 to 4S hours to cool one of those large boilers. Furthermore, it requires a considerable time to get up steam to do justice to the boilers. During all that time the boat is lying in port and expenses are running up. I am of the opinion, therefore, that it is a big drawback to these boats that the boilers have not a lead over the engines. The disadvantage would not be so great if they could use oil fuel, I am referring to boats that are using coal. There is another consideration, too. If the boilers had the lead I suggest, the boats could use slack instead of good coal. The firemen would have no difficulty in keeping up steam with slack coal, which is about one-third the price of first-class coal, and in that way a great saving could be made.
It has been suggested that these steamers should be provided with passenger accommodation. In my opinion they are not built for that purpose and never will be a success as passenger carriers. There is no doubt in my mind about that; and if any more money were invested to provide for passenger accommodation on these steamers it would be only so much more money thrown away.
Taking these things into consideration, I believe that the best thing that the government could do would be to get rid of the smaller boats as best they can. We have got into this mess and we must get out of it. But I want the' House to understand that the government is not the only one that has got into difficulties in connection with shipbuilding. There were some people in Vancouver who built boats for the government, and when the government refused to give any more orders they formed a company and built ships for themselves. Some of these ships cost over a million dollars, and one in particular was sold last fall, I think, for 8250,000, or less than one-quarter what it cost originally. Parliament should understand therefore that the government is not the only one that is faced with this proposition. I cannot see how these boats will ever pay running expenses, and when these ships can-
 .
not take care of themselves and pay the running charges, surely the sooner the government get rid of them the better it will be for the whole country. I do not propose to offer any opposition to this item, but I do think that the minister should give the House some guarantee that he will endeavour to get rid of the boats in whatever way he can before another session of parliament is called. We should not be asked to vote a sum of money year after year to keep up something that is of no benefit to the country. What right has this House to vote the money of the taxpayers each year in the way of a bonus to keep in operation these boats that are competing with ships owned by private companies? I do not think it is fair to the other companies. Those other companies have to pay their crews, and interest on their investment, and, in a great many cases, income tax. Why then should this government vote sums of the taxpayers' money year after year for the purpose of competing with private companies that are doing a legitimate business? I do not think it is right, and I certainly hope that before another session comes around the minister will see his way clear to have some at least of the boats disposed of.	*

I rise to apologize to the House for the statement I made last night which the minister referred to a moment ago -that freight was paid to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats on coal carried by them from Sydney to Montreal at the rate of 82.80 per ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It was a member over there who said it.

Somebody said it anyway, and I said so, too. The minister points out today that I made a mistake and that the freight rate charged was $1.50 per ton. Well, I have to apologize to the House because I made the rate too low. I do not know where the minister got his information, but if he will turn to the Auditor General's report for 1922 he will find the following at page W-116:
Freight on coal, Canadian Government Merchant Marine: Sydney to Levis, 3,110 tons at $4 per ton-
What!
Four dollars per ton, when other boats were carrying coal for $1.10 per ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: What year?

I am quoting from the Auditor General's report for the year ended March 31, 1922. Continuing my quotation:

Supply-Merchant Marine
Sydney to St. John and Halifax, 19,202 tons at $2.60; Louisburg to St. John and Halifax, 29,337 tons at $2.60.
I am quite sure that other boats would have carried this coal at half the rate to the two latter ports, and at less than half to Levis. And yet the minister says the coal was carried at a rate of $1.50 per ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We will have that checked up. The item referred to goes further back-
This is the last report of the Auditor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That would be for business done in 1920 I imagine. It goes back further than the business I was referring to, which was done in 1921. I thought that would be far enough back. The manager told me last night that he thought $1.50 was the rate. He telephoned to Montreal this morning and his figure was confirmed. It referred to 1921, a year later. I will have the item looked into; there may be some explanation of the very high rates quoted.

I just wanted to show that I
was right in my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

, Mr. MEIGHEN: Mr. Chairman, of all hon. members here I can make no pretence to any practical knowledge of either shipbuilding or the shipping business, but I think it is due to the House that some short review should be made of the history of the Canadian Government Mercantile Marine, to clear away any misconceptions that might arise from these discussions.
While I do not disagree-as I usually have to, very reluctantly

with everything said by the hon. member for Lunenburg, (Mr. Duff); because a part of his review of the history of the matter is not out of accord with my recollection-I fear the House would get the impression that something approaching insanity, something unaccompanied by the slightest sense of public duty, had animated- the late government in its mercantile marine policy, that in our hurry to get rid of all the funds of the country we had put them into expensive vessels which when built were not fitted to carry passengers, package freight, cattle or coal, indeed, were not much good for anything save as a spectacle of extravagance and waste; and that having committed this folly, we proceeded to add another, to seek to operate these vessels under a board, none of whose members had any financial interest in their operation.
I think hon. members are fairly well acquainted with what has taken place, and in that respect the hon. member for Lunenburg, to do him justice, was not grossly and violently wrong. It was in 1918 that the enterprise of shipbuilding was first launched upon. It was not in 1918 that the first public agitation to that end was commenced. Well I recall in years previous from the benches of the then opposition a determined campaign was opened to compel the government to establish for Canada a mercantile marine. The champion of that agitation he who was most eloquent and most persistent, he who excelled in both those qualities, was the Hon. William Pugsley, now seated in a less contentious post. Previous to that agitation we did not undertake the work. The demands upon the Treasury were very great, the prospect of a large government railway mileage was not immediate, the success of the German submarine campaign was much less a menace than it became later on, and the call for ships the world over was nothing at all in 1916 and 1917 to what it became in 1918.
In 1918, $25,000,000 was appropriated to help meet the situation on the part of Canada. The Prime Minister of the day came to parliament and secured approval of that appropriation, and he set out before the House the entire programme as then contemplated by the administration. Up to this point I do not think the two accounts of what has happened differ.
Previous to the armistice contracts were let for forty-five ships, and these included the smaller ships that are now the subject of so much discussion. These smaller ships at that time could be built quickly, they were needed quickly, they had a very, very pressing service immediately to perform, and therefore they were included in the ships first laid down. The contracts went on. In the spring of 1919, though the armistice had been signed and peace was almost certain to be declared, it became evident not only to this country, but, I think, to every other country that the need for ships was even greater than it had been twelve months before. When I say it became evident, I fortify the phrase by the assertion that every other country answered to the demand at least in equal degree proportionately to what this country did; some countries answered in much greater

Supply-Merchant Marine
proportion. I mention in this regard particularly the United States of America.
Then, in 1919, other circumstances came in sight of very great and immediate consequence relative to the shipbuilding programme. Not only was the world's shipping depleted and the world suffering seriously from such depletion at that time, but Canada, having already acquired at the close of 1917 the Canadian Northern Railway, had in view the acquirement of the Grand Trunk Railway. Indeed', its acquirement seemed to be inevitable by one process or the other. Hence there could be seen in view a tremendous railway system owned and operated by the government in competition with the other great Canadian transportation system, the Canadian Pacific Railway. There were other circumstances as well, the force of which does not now come home to the mind with the same weight and by anything like the same pressure with which it was brought home to the minds of hon. members of this House of all political persuasions in 1919. Those were the days of very rapid demobilization. Our soldiers were coming back by the hundreds of thousands, and the country was utterly unable to absorb with the speed of their return the men who had done service overseas. Unemployment is at all times a very serious subject matter for a government's consideration. But unemployment when suffered by men returning from a terrific conflict differs from other unemployment. The demand then must be met; public opinion will permit nothing but that it be met to the full power of the government. The pressure for these ends I can, of course, very easily recall; I was in the midst of it. I ask hon. gentlemen to keep in mind that pressure of that kind is a just pressure, and, what is more, it is an irresistible pressure. Money spent in providing employment, even if we assume it is spent in the construction of something of no great value, is not wholly money wasted; if we had not provided it in one form or the other we would have paid it out in cash. The situation had to be confronted and surmounted. It was confronted and surmounted, and the construction of more vessels was one of the methods by which this end was attained. Now, I have mentioned three circumstances; all were of consequence. Others I might review, but those three circumstances, I say, were of exceeding consequence indeed. I emphasize again that among the vessels first laid down, contracts for which were signed, executed and in process of completion at the time the armistice v7as signed, the smaller were included; a suffi-f.Mr. Meighen.]
cient number of the larger vessels for other purposes was not included in the first laid down. The government, therefore, in April, 1919, laid1 before parliament proposals for the construction, I think it was, of eighteen more -at all events, of the balance.
That is right; eighteen.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I ask hon. members to recall that included in that government were hon. members who now sit opposite; included in that government was the former leader of the Progressive party. All concurred in submitting to parliament proposals for that construction, and I do all of them justice when I say that they were moved to that view by the considerations I have sought now to impress again on the committee. Not only did we ask for the money for the purpose-that is to say, for such amount of it as could reasonably be expended in 1919-20, but we informed parliament of the character of the vessels to be constructed; informed parliament of all the details that parliament has a right in every case to be furnished with before being asked to approve of the proposal made. The approval was given in 1918; the approval was given in 1919, and I doubt if any subject matter' has ever been placed before this House that received in each case so unanimous an approval on the part of parliament as did the subject matter of our mercantile marine construction. In 1918 I can remember no dissentient note whatever. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. 4 p.m. Duff) refers to a doubt expressed by the then member for Red Deer. I do not dispute it. I have not had time to look it up; my recollection was that was in 1919 rather than 1918. However, beyond the doubt expressed by him, which, I think, was based on the view he so consistently held that everything except raising wheat could be done cheaper in England or Scotland than in Canada-outside of that I know of no dissentient or discordant note of any kind from any quarter in the Canadian House in either year. In such form the estimates passed and the contracts were subsequently let for these additional vessels. I ask hon. members to keep in mind this fact: Though the vote was passed the government was not bound to go ahead; the government had the authority of parliament to do so, but had circumstances altered it would have been quite justified in changing its policy and coming to parliament later with an explanation. But the circumstances that obtained in the fall and winter and spring of 1918-19 were just as pressing and just as powerful all through the summer of 1919.

I have carried the record of the decisions of parliament up to the spring of 1919. In that summer the balance of the contracts were let. In the spring of 1920, the government came to parliament again, not with any new proposals at all, but with an estimate of the amount that would be required to proceed with the work on the proposals that parliament had adopted the year before, the amount that would be required for the then ensuing year, because, of course, ships of the size then being built could not be constructed even in that year. Parliament voted that money. It was merely a vote carrying out the previous programme unanimously adopted, without a dissenting vote in the House of Commons. I think I am safe in saying, although I have not had time to review the debates of 1920 for the

purposes of this discussion, that there was no contention in the House even in 1920 against going on with works that were under way; nor was there reflection passed upon the wisdom of the course that had been adopted finally in the spring of 1919. The facts were that at that time other countries were excelling themselves in the same way; that the demand for space, instead of falling off, was as strong as ever; that though conditions in Canada were improving somewhat, the necessity for keeping employed those still at work on our ships, a large proportion of those men being returned men, was just as great and pressing as before. So the work proceeded, and it was almost completed in 1920, only a relatively very small appropriation, I do not know whether it was $2,000,000 or $3,000,000, being required in 1921. This appropriation was determinedly opposed. By this time changes had taken place in the whole mercantile work. By this time deflation was under way. By this time there was a surplus of ships. There was no demand any longer for more; indeed ships were a glut on the markets of the world. Certain hon. gentlemen then saw their chance, and they who had voted for the entire project and for its continuance, turned around and held parliament up in a determined effort to prevent the vote from going through.

I do not say that we could have had them in 1919; but we could have had them in 1920, and I am not sure that we could not have had them in 1919. I will tell my hon. friend why we did not. We felt that it was better at that time, when Britain and her allies were sadly in need of ships to make up what the German submarines had destroyed, to keep the docks for our own purposes. I well recall-and I say this with no idea of making a contentious matter of what the present Speaker said at chat time-the strong approval coming from the then hon. member for Maisonneuve because we did this with a policy of holding cur own ports and harbours for the construction of vessels for ourselves and our allies. Great Britain was building ships in Canada at that time through the agency of the Imperial Munitions Board.
This carries us through the programme of ship construction. Now it is said: "Very well; you were right so far as that goes; you did what the best minds and the best judgments in the world, trained and experienced in the subject, were doing at that time. But after they got through, you should have sold them when the price was high. You should not have started to operate them yourselves. You should not have formed a company to operate them. You should not have sought to operate them as a government enterprise. You should have sold them when the price was good and the selling was good." I admit that the selling was good and the price was high. Doubtless, even though we needed the ships later on, it would have paid to have sold them and later on to have bought others. I wonder if that is not the experience of everybody in this world? Is there in the world to-day a business that would not be far better off now if it had just sold its assets two or two and a half years ago and then bought what it needed later on? When did this demand arise in parliament for the sale of our ships? Did any hon. gentleman hear it in 1919 when some of the ships were on the way to completion, when some of them were completed? Did any hon. gentlemen hear it in 1920 when most of them were completed and when the company was formed, in operation, and showing a profit to this country? Nobody ever heard such a claim. The demand came, as it always comes in private life, after the event. You always know the market after the event. Then the complaint came that we should have known this before and sold when the price was good. But there are other considerations that affect a government than
244i
merely the level of the market. By this time we had acquired the Grand Trunk Railway; by this time we were owners of a system of 23,000 miles of railway, and what is more, we were in competition with the best organized, biggest and, perhaps, best managed single business enterprise in the known world, the Canadian Pacific railway. We were in severe competition with them in every line of activity, and we found our competitor with 440,000 tons of shipping at its command ready to serve its system in this country, ready to drain from all the ports of the world the world's business to the Canadian Pacific in Canada. Was it to be thought that we were to face that competition, and while we were addressing ourselves to facing it, disarm ourselves of what mercantile marine we had? Certainly, if we had known the market and known we could have later on bought more cheaply, that would have been the course. But aside from a prevision of the market, I do not see that any argument could be made that we should have adopted any such policy. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have to-day in their annual statement a mercantile marine asset of some $59,000,000 at cost of construction. The Canadian Pacific fortunately built their vessels at a much cheaper cost than we did. Why? Because they built them sooner; they built them before the war, in the main, although it is true they have built some since. But their average cost of construction is below ours, their tonnage being above ours. The Canadian Pacific Railway to-day have, proportionately to their mileage, far more mercantile marine tonnage than have the National Railways. I doubt not they have double the amount: I think they have double, proportionately to their mileage, the tonnage tlat the National Railways have.
Some complaint, however, is made. It is said: "You did not build cheaply enough; you should have built by tender, and you could have justified your vessels at the time you built them because it was a war necessity. When the whole enterprise was entered upon you could have got them built more cheaply." Well, I venture to say this, and I am glad of the chance to say it in justice to an hon. gentleman who is no longer a member of this House: No enterprise of the Canadian people was ever better managed from a business point of view than was the construction of the Canadian Mercantile Marine, and I invite hon. gentlemen opposite, if they have any question as to that, to be good enough to follow their policy of commission-making just a little further and appoint one, two, or
Supply-Merchant Marine

three experienced shipbuilding men-and they can appoint a judge of their own choosing at the head-to investigate the whole subject of the Canadian Mercantile Marine I would welcome, and every hon. member on this side of the House would welcome, such an investigation; and certainly no one in this Dominion would welcome it with more avidity than the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Our Mercantile Marine was not built by tender for the simple reason that it could not be done. You cannot let by tender for the building of ships when you have fourteen docks in Canada, all of which must be engaged; nor can you build at the same price in one as you can in another. What country in the world does build its ships by tender? I do not know of any. I know that when we were building our 65 vessels, the United States were building 1,553, and they did not do the work by tender. Great Britain was building too at a very rapid rate, but she was not building by tender. We asked for the construction of a vessel of a certain type; we asked for quotations on that type of vessel to be built at a certain place; and we did not accept the lowest quotation. In every case, I think, the lowest we considered too high, and after the lowest was in a price was fixed and the builders were told that if they could not accept that price they could not get the work. The result was that we built our marine at an average cost of $191 per ton at the same time that the United States were building ships of poorer quality as the event shows, at $50 to $100 per ton more. At the same time, too, Great Britian was huilding at a cost equal to our own.

I admire the ingenuousness of the reply. Now what about the quality of the ships at the prices paid for them? I have read a speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who has become an expert on the subject of shipbuilding and the use of ships. I had lots of time and I read the speech; and one would gather from it that these were ships of a very poor quality. There was nothing that the hon. gentleman knew of which they could carry at all; at least I did not come across, anywhere

Sujrply-Merchant Marine
in his speech, anything to indicate that he thought they were fit for any purpose whatever. And I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) this afternoon. Does anyone imagine that the government of this country put $70,000,000 into ships without getting at least the best opinion at its command as to the nature of the ships required? Does anyone suppose that the government did all this without having availed itself of the best inspectors to supervise the execution of the work and to pass upon the soundness of the design? If hon. members have any doubt and believe that there was carelessness in that regard, again I invite them to institute an inquiry, and I venture to say that they will find that no better ships were built by any country or any individual firm than the ships that were built by us, nor were there any ships more suited to the needs of the time.

speechtext: What are they suited for?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: SITTING SUSPENDED FOR ROYAL ASSENT TO BILLS
speechtext: They are suited for anything. What are they not suited for? We are told that they cannot carry package freight. Well, twenty of them were specially built to carry package freight. Of these, 18 have 'tween decks for the purpose, and 2 of them have three decks. They were built for package freight, and built by the best designers whom we knew anything about.

subsubtopic: SITTING SUSPENDED FOR ROYAL ASSENT TO BILLS
speechtext: Can they carry cattle?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: SITTING SUSPENDED FOR ROYAL ASSENT TO BILLS
speechtext: They were not fitted to carry cattle and they were not carrying cattle because there were no cattle to carry. But all they need is stanchions for the purpose, and they will carry cattle the same as any other ships. I do not believe we are getting the benefit of these ships that we ought to get. I never have very much faith in an enterprise that is being managed by those unsympathetic to it. Up to the time we got the Grand Trunk into the system there was some excuse for the Grand Trunk business going to an American line-the White Star line, but since then I do not know of any excuse; I would like to hear of one if there is any. The Canadian Fisher, Captain Fergus Ferguson, proved to be a stout ship and weathered the gale [DOT]wonderfully well. All the boat covers were ripped free, while the canvas dodgers on the bridge were torn to pieces. One piece held on to a stanchion on Monkey Island and the force of the blow bent the upright. The heavy plate glass windows on the wings of the bridge were shattered into little pieces. Some damage was done to the Marconi house and the eng.ne room telegraph on the poop deck was wrecked.
There were only two casualties, a fireman receiving a scalp wound after having been pitched against some fittings, while Mr. Stoddard, the second officer, was struck by the end of a broken signal halliard, which whipped across his face and left him a cut and a black eye.
The Fisher was near Bermuda when the cyclonic gale broke and Captain Ferguson swung around so as to give the ship plenty of sea room. The wind started out of the northeast and swung around the compass, the Fisher shouldering her way around with the wind. She was driven at full speed and made about a knot an hour, meanwhile being driven thirty miles sideways.
Calm Night Followed
The wind blew with indescribable fury, whipping heavy rain across the mountainous seas. It was an amazing revelation of the power of an angry sea. After the gale had blown over and while the sea was yet running high, the sun came out in the afternoon and was followed by a glorious starlit night.
The Fisher had been warned of the approach of the cyclonic gale by heavy seas and also by wireless. The barometer dropped very rapidly, falling to 28.10, which is a very low mark. The barometer rose as rapidly as it fell.
On arrival at Hamilton the passengers subscribed to a memorial to Captain Ferguson expressing appreciation of his seamanship, courage and resourcefulness, and also praising the actions of the other officers, the crew and more particularly the engine room staff.

It is easier to say these things on the outside looking in than it is to do them on the inside looking out. First as to the stability of the ship, I have never heard any person question the stability of these ships that form the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Whether it was wise to build them or not, so far as I have been able to find out, they were built well. The United States constructed a large number of ships. I had the honour of being at the launching of some of them that never got any further than the bay in which they were launched. I refer to the wooden ships. The United States are in a great dilemma now with a large number of ships on their hands, with overhead charges piling up, with interest accumulating and no business for many of them. The head of the Shipping board, Albert D. Lasker, has made a report to the President that might be of interest. I will not read it, but I will give just a short synopsis of it. He recommends the formation, for the operation of 450 ships, of eighteen subsidiary companies with a central company to which these eighteen subsidiary companies will be responsible. That w'ould, I think, be 25 ships to a company, if each company had the same number of ships. But the division is not made in that way, as I understand the matter; but rather the ships on each route will be managed by a company, and the 450 ships are thus divided. It is interesting to know that Mr. Lasker, at the conclusion of his report, advised the government of the United States that they should continue to keep in mind the ultimate destiny of the ships, and that was the return of them to private ownership. That may take many years, and the life of the ships may be pretty well exhausted before that time arrives. In the meantime, the United States is endeavouring to make these ships useful and self-sustaining so far as possible. This much must be remembered: Supposing we sold all the ships-and I am in favour of
selling some of the smaller ones-that would reduce our annual interest charge, but it would not wipe it out; we would have an annual interest charge to all eternity on the amount of our loss. So, as regards that, selling these ships would not rid us of that annual expenditure.
A question was raised by my hon. friend as to the speed of the larger ships. It is true that in tests they did run up to 13^ knots an hour, but no ship can well be run in fair weather and bad weather up to its full test, because that would be very expensive. For instance, as regards a locomotive on one of our express or freight trains, sometimes a difference of ten miles an hour in speed will nearly double the consumption of coal. There is a limit to which a locomotive or a boiler can be driven; if you go beyond that limit, you increase the cost very much more materially than by pushing it up to a certain point. But the average rate of the vessels in fair weather and bad weather is from 10 to 11^ knots an hour. Hi knots, I think, being the speed of the two larger vessels. Freight shippers contend that for perishable goods that speed is not sufficient, but that the ships should have a speed of several knots an hour more than that in order to carry perishable goods across the ocean. Whether that be true or not, I am not an expert and I cannot say.

In fact, Sir Henry Thornton and every one of the directors with whom I have conversed are strongly of opinion that we ought to keep the larger boats and sell the smaller ones, and they are very sympathetic in the belief that the larger boats are very useful. I think, before the Grand Trunk came into the organization, the Canadian Northern had a working arrangement with the Cunard line. Now they have the Cunard and the White Star. I do not want to tell tales out of school, but I might intimate to the members of the committee that the returns from some of the routes are looking much better this year up to date than last year. It is true that last year was a fairly disastrous year for shipping, and many of the larger companies lost money. I will not give any details, but I am informed that some companies that we imagine are making large amounts of money on certain routes, last year lost very large amounts of money on those routes. Unquestionably the small ships are very staunch ships, but on the Great Lakes this is what they have to compete with. Further than that, some of the men who know the shipping history in the provinces down by the sea have urged upon me that we should preserve our Government Merchant Marine as a safeguard against the shipping trust-shall I call it?-which has grown up on the Atlantic seaboard. They say that some years ago a great many Canadian seamen were practically driven from Canadian waters because of the encouragement given to other boats, ordinarily called "Norwegian" boats, which were then introduced. Later the same group who had assisted the Norwegians became interested in steel, coal and other industrial concerns and were given special consideration at the expense of Canadian seamen. Still later, oriental crews were employed in the coastwise trade. It also should be pointed out particularly that some of these same big interests are today operating on the Great Lakes, as has been revealed in the reports of the commission investigating those matters. It would appear that if we are to prevent a monopoly of the financial and industrial interests which might very readily control the shipping both on the lakes and on the ocean, we shall have to own and control our own ships. We need, of course, in addition, a great deal more in the way of inspection, and also the services of some commission which will deal with the whole question of freight rates. There may be, as pointed out, the advisability of getting rid of some of these ships. Undoubtedly we ought to mark their present values down to present market prices. Some hon. members tell us that these ships are of very little use, and that they would have to be sold for very little. I suggest they be marked down to the fair market value of to-day, and then we
can treat with the profit and loss on that basis, not on the basis of any inflated or fictitious war value. These are details of administration but I should urge that we would do nothing whatever to impair the present service or make it difficult to carry out the underlying principle of government ownership and control.

subsubtopic: SITTING SUSPENDED FOR ROYAL ASSENT TO BILLS
speechtext:
I do not wish to unduly
detain the committee as I understand the minister is anxious to get away and I think he has been very patient throughout this discussion. But I wish to enter my protest against the proposed sale of twenty-seven ships of the Canadian Mercantile Marine. I have had twenty-five years' experience as a harbour commissioner and solicitor for vessel owners in the district from which I come and I wish to say that if the National Railway system is ever to become a success it must have lake and ocean services. One of the main reasons why the Canadian Pacific Railway has been such a striking success is because it has vessels engaged in the ocean and lake service as feeders. It is now proposed to sell these twenty-seven ships. Why do the management not sell their hotel and railway services also? If they are going to get rid of one agency for the building up of their business, why not dispose of them all? For my part I would not sell a tug, or a scow, or a dredge on the strength of the information that has been placed before the committee during this debate. I will go further and say that I do not believe the proposed sale commends itself to the wisdom and judgment of the country. The people who are concerned in shipments on the Great Lakes to-day want competition. A commission has conducted an inquiry into lake freight rates and practically before its report has been brought down, certainly before it has ever been considered by the House, and after the commission has taken considerable evidence, the recommendation is made that these twenty-seven ships be sold. These vessels were not built altogether for

use to-day; they were intended to meet the needs of the future. I do not know of any other country in the world that is proposing to dispose of the ships in its possession in the manner that is contemplated here. Of what avail is the expenditure which Canada has made on its inland harbours, its ocean ports, and its canals if, before we have actually established the necessary ocean and lake services that are so urgently required, we cripple one of the agencies necessary to bring about cheaper transportation? With all due respect to the gentlemen who compose the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Sir Henry Thornton is not a "cure all" for the transportation ills of,this country, far from it, some of the things recommended by the management of the National Railways and Merchant Marine do not commend themselves to us on this side of the House. How is it that so many private people all over Canada and the United States want to buy these vessels? It is said that these ships cannot navigate the lakes. I would point out that nine of them were built at Colling-wood, others at Port Arthur, and others again at Toronto, Midland and other places and they can do lake work on the Great Lakes. I wish to enter my emphatic protest against the proposed sale. I do so as the representative of an inland port which is spending twenty-six millions on harbour improvements.
As showing the need for improved transportation facilities on the lakes, I would point out that there is a Kirkwood shed in Toronto to-day twice the size of this chamber which is so full of freight that no more can be squeezed into it. The Kirkwood Company have illustrated with one vessel the success which can be made in operating on the lakes. They have applied to the government to be allowed to take over two or three more vessels, having demonstrated to the municipalities along the shore of lake Ontario that they can successfully manage lake shipping. I am very much surprised at the action of the government in recommending this sale. Stress has been laid upon the fact that these ships were built during the war and some ask why they were built at all. This is not relevant but they were built for war emergency, to add to shipping tonnage and help unemployment.
During the years 1916, 1917, and 1918 the unemployment conditions were such that the shipbuilding industry was a blessing to the large cities of Canada. That industry gave employment to twenty-six different classes of labour including ship carpenters, pattern makers, wheelwrights, engineers, skilled plate

Supply-Merchant Marine
workers, and boiler makers. They were all skilled workers and the most of them consisted of returned soldiers. During their service at the front they were only paid $1.10 a day and on returning to Canada were badly in need of employment. That is one of the reasons why so many of these ships were built. I think the difficulty in the way of the successful operation of these ships would be overcome if the government would engage the services of practical marine men. The whole of the vessels in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine could then be re-routed in such a way as to give results that would not only pay the fixed charges but leave a handsome profit.
It has been said that public ownership is responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves in this matter. That is not the case. If these ships were re-routed in the coasting and lake trade, put to other uses and given a fair trial, it would be seen after the lapse of two or three years what a great success would be achieved. The Canadian Pacific Company has for years had an admirably managed and most successful service on the ocean and on the upper lakes. The Canada Steamship Company has also been operating a lake passenger and freight service. The operation of its ships in the Niagara district and on the St. Lawrence has been a success. Unfortunately this company has frozen out competitors on a number of routes, for example, on the north shore of lake Ontario between Toronto and Belleville. Having freed themselves from competition they can charge whatever they like in the way of passenger and freight rates. The vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine offered us the prospect of relief from these excessive charges but the action of the government seems likely to prevent its realization.
I do not wish to occupy an undue amount of time-I think the House has sat far too long; I would not complain if prorogation were taking place to-night-the federal Australian parliament can do its work in ten weeks, so should we-but I would direct attention to page 51 of the report on lake freight rates wherein it is set forth that a monopoly exists, that there is no competition at the present time, and that conditions are not what they should be. The lake ports are congested, and there is no regulation of the rates on grain, iron ore, coal and package freight. The more I study this problem the more I am convinced that a mistake has been made in regard to the disposition of these ships. I repeat, they were not built simply for the purposes of to-day. What was contemplated was to provide for the needs of the future and if we part with these vessels now we will be making a terrible mistake. No other country in the world is taking such a step as that. Great Britain was wise enough to foresee the possibilities that underlay the combination of coal and steel, and the great part transportation facilities would play in their development.
The greatest industrial expansion of England did not come from Cobdenism and free trade, but from the union of steel and coal. The great British navy started and as a merchant marine fleet. Seventy-five years ago men of war were added to it. There were no dreadnoughts in those days. Drake, Frobisher and Hawkins were men of the merchant marine, and they went out to the seven seas of the world and made England the great maritime country it is to-day. The Americans have taken a leaf out of their book. They had a conference in Washington. Did they adhere to the terms of the conference? No. Have all the war plants been reduced to a peace standing? No. I know that many of the shipbuilding plants have been busy lately constructing ships on the Atlantic seaboard-war plants turned into peace plants and building ships for their merchant marine. You will see they are busy building ships by private contract for private owners and also building some for the government. Very shortly the United States will go out to the seven seas of the world, and they are going out to the seven seas to get the balance of trade; they will catch up with England's merchant marine, surpass her and will they hope become the mistress of the seas, so far as the merchant marine is concerned.
In conclusion, I do not agree with this recommendation. We have spent, I think,. $900,000,000 jn direct and indirect aid to the railways of Canada. The deficits-were last night placed by the minister' at about $6,000,000 and all we are asked to vote to-night is $1,500,000. I think that all the money that requires to be voted here to-night is just sufficient to meet the actual out-of-pocket charges, because you do not require to vote depreciation and interest-on railways or the merchant fleet, which you own yourself. Therefore, I say the country can very well afford a million and a half this year to give the Merchant Marine another trial for two or three more years, not only on the ocean services but on the lake services. I believe if the government gives it a trial it will get an increased business; if the ships are re-routed,

Supply-Merchant Marine
they will get not only the coasting trade, but the smaller vessels will get the business on the Great Lakes. There is a great opening for these freighters on the lakes. They can come down through lake Erie. and lake Ontario, down the St. Lawrence and go out along the seaboard and also do a coasting trade. That was shown by the report laid before the government a year or two ago. Is it a proper thing to sell ships when the market is flooded and gutted? A large number of boats along the Hudson are offered for sale but the owners will not sell them just now because they hope to get a better price than that offered. At present the market is glutted and it is no time to make the sale which has been proposed. The Merchant Marine can be utilized to carry coal and can be converted into ships which will carry cattle to the Old Country, and other packet freight from the Maritime provinces to the head of the lakes including coal.
It has been said that the Merchant Marine representatives sat in at the meetings of the Atlantic Combine, and they have been criticized for it. Notwithstanding that, the head of the Canadian National Railways becomes a director of the great monopoly, the Canada Steamship Company. Sir Henry Thornton cannot serve two masters. He never should have become a director of this large shipping concern, the Canada Steamships Company, which froze out all the smaller'companies carrying freight to Buffalo and Toronto from the head of the lakes. Yet the government allows one of its National Railway directors to become the head of this monopoly. It has been stated that he becomes such a director because the National Railways fh&s an exchange of traffic with the Canada ,'Steamship Company. It has an exchange *of traffic with the Michigan Central, Lake ;Shore and Baltimore and Ohio. Is it right that Sir Henry Thornton should then also become a director of these three American railways as well? I believe it is wrong and that the people will not approve of it.
I wish to utter my protest against the proposal before the Chair to-night. I believe the time will come when we will see that it is a mistake. These ships were built for Canada, to give the National Railways a chance, and to act as feeders for them on the lakes and the ocean, in order to see what could be done in an economical way by assisting water-borne traffic to reduce the great freight charges which the people out West and throughout Canada are paying to-day.
fMr. Church.]

speechtext:
Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the second reading of Bill No. 205 to amend the Pension Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 3-Disabilities in respect of which pensions claimed.

I think perhaps a slight amendment would improve this section. The section says:
Pensions shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability resulting from injury or disease or an aggravation thereof, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A of this act.
That refers to disability pensions which are always payable to the man himself. I think if the words "or in respect of" were struck

Pension Act
out of the first line, it would be an improvement. Likewise on page 2, at the bottom, I find the words-
And in respect of members of the forces who have died, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule B of this act, when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to military service as such.
I think if the words-
In respect of wh-ich the application for pension is made
-are struck out in that place, and also the same repetition in lines 5 and 6, the clause will be made clearer. I throw out this suggestion to the minister for what it is worth. I have studied the clause with some care.

It looks as though it would cut out soldiers' dependents if you cut out the words "in respect of" in the first line of clause 3 (a). As proposed to be amended it would read:
Pension shall be awarded to members of the forces.
The expression "in respect of" would refer to pensions in respect of their dependents. I may be wrong, but that is my understanding.

The pensions in schedule A are pensions payable to the men themselves, not payable to dependents at all. The pensions in schedule B, which is referred to in the following part of the same clause, are pensions payable to dependents. The only man who can receive a pension under schedule A of the act is the man himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I beg to disagree with my hon. friend-I am sorry. Schedule A refers to the men themselves, but it also refers to:
Additional pensions for children for above ranks, first child, second child-
And so on. Children are dependents. That is why the words "in respect of" are in the clause.
And the pensioner's wife and children are entitled to a certain proportion of the pension as well as the pensioner himself, and this would be cut out if those words were removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is correct.

The first line of paragraph (c) of clause 3, subclause (1) reads:
An applicant shall not be deprived of pension.
He is only an applicant, and until he gets his pension, he cannot be deprived of. it.
. Would it not be better to use the word "denied"? I think that would make the clause
clearer. The remainder of the paragraph describes the obstacle that will not stand in his way to a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Of course we have the same purpose in view. Does my hon. friend believe, if we replace the words "deprived of" by the word "denied," that would make the clause clearer?
Yes, and less capable of technical construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no objection to the change in this case.
I move that the words " deprived of " be struck out in the first line of clause 3, subclause (1) (c), and that the word "denied" be substituted therefor.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Clause 3 (b) "pre-enlistment disabilities," provides in the fifth line that: No pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which at such time was wilfully concealed.
It seems to me, if any man has served in the theatre of war and has passed before the army officials and the doctors, the onus should not be on the man himself. I do not see that it is possible for any man to conceal wilfully some disability and pass before three or four doctors at least three times before he gets into the actual theatre of war. If such a condition did exist, if those doctors failed in their duty to find such a disability and the man actually worked in the theatre of war, the responsibility is not on the man himself, but on the doctors and officials who allowed him to pass.

What would the hon. gentleman do in the case of a man who went overseas with a glass eye and who did not inform the doctors that he had a glass eye? The doctors, perhaps, did not notice it, or if they did, they passed it over. Would the hon. member grant this man a pension for the loss of an eye if he returned in the same condition as when he went over?
If the army had any doctors who passed a man with a glass eye and who had no more insight into human nature the blame is upon the government.
Would the hon. gentleman give the soldier a pension?
Who is to prove that he had! a glass eye before?

I am giving an extremecase. I know of the case of a man who had a glass eye and who went overseas. He is in
Pension Act

perfect health, and he has the same glass eye as the one he went over with. I do not think he is entitled to a pension.

Is he claiming a pension
under the disability clause?
Not at all.
Then the case settles itself.

If we are at the end of section 3, I should like to submit to the committee an amendment to be inserted after section 3 as section 3A dealing with the question of attributability. In paragraph (a) of sub-clause (1) of clause 3 of this bill, we find the words:
Was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
There arises the very important question of what is commonly - called "attributability." Around that has been built up by the Pension board a procedure in which frequently the onus of proof in such cases, as has been contended by many, is placed upon the applicant. That is, when you have a case of some doubt, like neurasthenia or tuberculosis or something of that kind, the applicant puts in an application, and although the Pension board say that there is no question of onus of proof, yet the experience of many, including my own, shows in fact that there is, according to the interpretation of the act by the Pension board. They say that, in their opinion, "attributability to service" does not exist. The same problem arose in Great Britain, and there they passed a special act this year. I have taken out the main section of that to add as clause 3A to this bill. It is of such importance that I think it is wise to read the proposed amendment carefully in full to the committee so that the}'' will understand it. I propose to add as clause 3A:
3A. For the purpose of the Pension Act and amendments thereto and notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the provisions of the said act and amendment thereto, or any other act, where a member of the force who has left the naval, military or air force service is, or at any time after the date of his leaving that service has been found to be suffering from tuberculosis, neurasthenia, cancer, or any other disease or incapacity which could reasonably be attributed to war service, such member shall be deemed to be suffering from a disease attributable to, or aggravated by naval, military or air force service, as the case may be, unless or until it is shown that the tuberculosis or neurasthenia or cancer or other disease or incapacity was neither attributable to nor aggravated by, such service; and for the purpose of this provision, acceptance for such service shall be conclusive that at the time of joinog such service the officer or man was not suffering from any such disease or incapacity.
That is practically the provision in the English act which seeks to overcome this difficulty. It will be seen that the applicant

must first establish a reasonable case; he must first submit to the Board of Pension
Commissioners a prima facie case. The applicant is in a somewhat awkward situation. A widow, for example, may not have available the evidence which the law would make a conclusive case. So that when it is shown that a man enlisted as Al, and apparently was in good physical condition when he went overseas, that he did service, and perhaps was given some hospital attention, and then returning was suddenly found to have tuberculosis, he could perhaps show a prima facie case. The effect of this amendment would be that unless the board could show by evidence or medical testimony that the applicant or the person suffering from any disease or incapacity did not have such disease or incapacity, proof of which must be established in order to comply with the provisions of the act, then the applicant must be entitled to the benefit of the doubt. I do not know whether I have made myself perfectly clear. However, let me state the matter again to put it beyond all possibility of misunderstanding. If it appears that the applicant has all the material facts in his favour, then it is to be presumed that he has a prima facie case. The board may show by medical testimony, or in any other manner consistent with the evidence in cases of this kind, that the applicant is not entitled to a pension because, perhaps, the disease or incapacity was not attributable to war service, or for a number of other reasons which would deprive him of his pension under the provisions of the act. I beg to move the amendment which I have read, a copy of which I am sending to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I must read it a couple of times before I can say anything upon it; it is rather complicated.

Tubercular patients, I think, have given to the Pension board more worry than any other class of applicants; and when I say that I simply mean that their cases have been involved in so much medical technicality that, I am sorry to say, I do not think tubercular applicants have received that fair meed of justice which they deserved at the hands of their countrymen. I am afraid, however, that my hon. friend (Mr. Ladner) is going very far in his amendment. If he would just confine it to tubercular and cancerous patients, I would strongly support the amendment, but when he adds the words "or other disease or incapacity" it seems to me he is going far afield. My idea in rising now, though, is to ask the minister to inform the

Pension Act
committee whether the amendments to the Pension Act are in any way loosening up in regard to tubercular patients. I understand that this is one of the very serious questions which the commission, whose report has been submitted, have had to deal with. I have not had time to read the amendments through, and the minister might enlighten the committee as to how tubercular patients are to be benefited under them to any greater extent than they were under the original act.

Hon. members
have received a circular from the Dominion Alliance. Have they been consulted in reference to the drafting of the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Everybody has been consulted. In reply to my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) I might make a few observations in reference to the principle of the bill. I might have stated -them before the Speaker left the chair, but I will repeat now what I said two or three days ago when the Pension estimates were under consideration. When the original act was passed, what is known as the "insurance principle" was embodied in it. The insurance principle means that a man who served between the declaration of war and the declaration of peace will be pensioned for any disability which has been incurred by him during his service, whether such disability is or is not attributable to that service. It was, as Mr. Rowell said in the House when the bill was introduced in 1919, an insurance principle which was larger than the principle of any pension law of any other country in the worid. I repeat, that clause 11 of the bill of 1919-which is the vital clause because it provides for the awarding of pensions-stipulates that a pension should be awarded for or in respect of any disability when such disability not only was attributable to service but had been incurred during service although not directly related thereto. Let me give the House an example. Two soldiers are in charge of a truck loaded with munitions on the way to the front to serve a battery. They stop the truck and one of the men jumps off, crosses the ditch, runs into an orchard, climbs a tree and picks some apples. Whilst doing so he falls and breaks a limb. This is a disability incurred on service but not attributable to service. The other man remaining on the truck has the misfortune to lose an arm and a leg through an enemy aeroplane bombing the truck and exploding the munitions. This man's disability is attributable to service as such. Hon. members will see the difference. In 1919, when the first Pension Act was introduced by the Hon. Mr. Rowell, it was stated that any disability incurred during service would be pensioned. This principle disappeared one year later by the amending act of 1920. I do not want to delay the House unduly, but I think this explanation will enable hon. members to understand the purpose of the present amendments.
When in 1919 Mr. Rowell was in charge of the legislation then introduced he was asked what it meant. In reply he said:
Under the law as it now stands-
As he presented it.
-our pension system is really an insurance.
Then Mr. Griesbach-now Senator Gries-bach-asked him:
Why introduce that element?
Mr. Rowell: Our law as it stands is broader than the pension law in any other country, so far as we know. The insurance feature which I have mentioned is not in any other law, so far as I am aware. In that respect we give the soldier the benefit of insurance during the whole period of the war.
Mr. Griesbach: That is the principle that underlies all pensions.
Mr. Rowell: No. The principle underlying all pension is disability due to service. Under our pension law, if a soldier contracts disease under a purely normal condition having no relation at all to service, he becomes entitled to pension. It is really an insurance system.
The law was passed in that form, so that from September 1, 1919, to September 1 of the following year, when the law was amended as I shall point out in a few moments, the principle underlying the Pension Act was that any disability incurred during service was pensionable.
Let us come to one year later when the act was amended.
What year was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The year 1920. In that year old section 11 was repealed, and the following was substituted therefor:
The commision shall award pensions to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A of this act, and in respect of members of the forces who have died, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule B of this act, when the disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to military service.
The first act read:
Was attributable to or was incurred or aggravated during military sendee.
When this was proposed to the Pension committee-of which I was a member-the representatives of the Pension board were asked whether this amendment would affect the members of the Canadian Expeditionary
3S52
Pension Act

Force, and the answer was, "No, the C.E.F. men are not going to be affected." In order to make my assertion clearer, let me read a few words from the evidence given before that committee by representatives of the Pension board. A question was asked Dr. Burgess-who is one of the medical advisers of the Pension board-as to what would be the effect of the amendment. His answer was:
Prior to the late war pensions were paid for disabilities attributable bo service-
Prior to the late war.

Suppose a person who

In the following year, 1921, the act was made a little bit narrower by the addition of the two words "as such" to clause 11, meaning that no pension could be awarded unless the disability or the death in respect to which the application was made was attributable to military service as such. Now,
I	must go back for a moment to the act of 1919, because there is a paragraph in section'
II	with which we must be familiar if we are to understand clearly what has happened. The paragraph to which I refer is as follows:
Provided, further, that when a member of the forces has suffered disability or death after the declaration of peace, no pension shall be paid unless such disability was incurred or aggravated or such death occurred, as the direct result of military service.
