The proclamation of peace took place on the thirty-first of August, 1921, and the Pension board thereupon proceeded to interpret the act as it had been amended in 1920 and 1921. In other words, we were face to face with a situation which was absolutely untenable, namely, that if a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force died five minutes before midnight on the thirty-first of August,
1921,	his dependents were pensionable, because his death was the result of disability incurred on service but not attributable to service, whereas if he had the misfortune to die ten minutes later, five minutes after midnight, his dependents could not be pensioned, because he had died after the declaration of peace, though of the same disability incurred in the same manner. The Pension board then sent out a circular or a minute in which they informed all the medical advisers that in future pensions should

Pension Act
be awarded in respect to disability or death only when such disability or death was attributable to military service as such. During the last months of 1921 this new principle was applied not only to members of the permanent force but to members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and numerous complaints on that account came from returned men in all parts of the country. They were especially numerous and pronounced during the first months of the year 1922, culminating in the presentation of their case by representatives of the veterans in June of last year and the decision to appoint a royal commission to investigate these matters. Now the royal commission has held its investigation on that phase of the subject, and its report is to the effect that there has been a breach of contract with members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force in regard to pensions; that it was made clear in 1920 that any amendment then passed was to be applied
9 p.m. not to the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force but only to members of the permanent force, and the commissioners recommended that the act should be restored as it was in 1919. The purpose of this bill .therefore, is to restore the insurance principle as embodied in the act introduced by Mr. Rowell and passed by the House in that year.
Now, how could we do this? We amend the interpretation clause; we say that the "war" means that period between the fourth day of August, 1914, and the thirty-first day of August, 1921, both days inclusive. Then we drafted a new clause 11. I say "we," because I did not myself undertake to draft the clause. I knew what the spirit of it should be, and I asked more than one experienced draftsman to draft it for me. I have submitted the redrafted clause to a number of eminent lawyers and they say it carries out the purpose the royal commission had in mind and the desires of the veterans generally, and that it fulfils the meaning of the act of 1919. We decided that clause 11 should be in two parts, subsection 1 and subsection 2, that subsection 1 should deal with men who had rendered service during the war and subsection 2 with men who had rendered service after the war. If hon. gentlemen will refer to the bill before them they will see that clause 3 reads in part as follows:
(11). (1) In respect of military service rendered during the war,-
If you read paragraph (a) from first to last you will see that it restores the insurance principle. It says:
(a) Pensions shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability resulting from injury or disease or an aggravation thereof, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A of this act, and in respect of members of the forces who have died, in accordance with the rates set out in schedule B of this Act, when the disability resulting from injury or disease or the aggravation thereof in respect of which the application for pension is made or the injury or disease or the aggravation thereof resulting in the death in respect of which the application for pension is made, was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
This is a complete restoration of the insurance principle as it existed in 1919. It is in the opinion of the royal commission, I believe it is in the opinion of the veterans generally, and, as far as I can judge, it carries out the purpose absolutely. Now, the second subsection says:
In respect of military service rendered after the war.
That is in respect of service rendered by men who remained in the force after the declaration of peace. I think that "force" must mean the permanent force, or perhaps some other body of men in the militia still serving although the war was over. Now in respect of these men it is said that-
Pensions shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability-
I will not read the whole clause-when the disability or death-
-was attributable to military service as such.
So, repeating myself and in order to make myself perfectly clear to hon. members, there are two classes of men: Men who served between the 4th August, 1914 and the 31st August, 1921, when the declaration of peace was made, for whom the insurance principle is restored, and a second class of men who served after the declaration of peace and who are still, I believe, in service but in regard to whom no pension shall be awarded unless the disability is attributable to military service as such. There are a number of subsections but these, of course, extend the principle.
I understand the minister to point out that there is really no change in the spirit of the act itself. This is simply clearing up the spirit of the act. Am I correct?

I stated at that time, and I state again now, that in my opinion the country owes to every returned soldier the fullest and the best treatment which can possibly be given, compatible with the resources of the country; I think I used the words "the future welfare of the nation." I have not changed my mind in the very slightest degree since last year. I think that every returned man, and the dependent of every returned man who has died, should be given, not only a perfectly fair and equitable deal by this House and by the country, but in addition should be given the most generous treatment that can possibly be accorded him. On the other hand, I think you, Mr. Chairman, and all hon. members will admit that when any claim is made against the country, no matter from what source that claim may come, there should be a certain amount of substantiation, a certain amount of evidence adduced in support of that claim before the money of the people is paid out. That theory holds as regards returned men the same as regards any other citizens in Canada, excepting in this, that as regards returned men, any claim that they may have, direct or indirect, must and should be and, I am certain, is intended to be, treated with the utmost generosity in every particular.
The minister has explained to the committee to-night section 11 of the act. That section is the governing section of the whole act. He has explained the difference between the insurance principle and the "due to service" principle. He has told the committee that, under the act of 1919 the principle at that time was the insurance principle. Subsequently, in 1920, that principle was made the "due to service" principle. There was a very great distinction, and the distinction was this, that under the insurance principle any disability of any kind incurred on service, the slightest aggravation of any disability the seedier had was pensionable in full and his dependents also could have a pension. Under the "due to service" principle, the soldier had to show that the disability from which he was suffering was due to military service. That is now entirely wiped out and the insurance principle is returned to. Any disability from which a soldier may be suffering up to the 31st day of August, 1921, is pensionable, providing that it was incurred on service, or in any way attributable to

service, or in any way aggravated during military service. Those words are very significant, and they are premising the remarks which I intend to make on the amendment which my hon. friend (Mr. Ladner) has brought forward to-night. I want the committee to bear in mind the date whereof I speak, namely the 31st August, 1921. The war ended substantially on the 11th November, 1918. The Canadian Expeditionary Force was disbanded-I am speaking from memory now and I should like to be corrected il I am wrong-if I mistake not, on the 31jt December, 1920. All the soldiers were disbanded at that time; but notwithstanding that disbanding, the "incurred on service" principle, or the insurance principle is brought along to the 31st August, 1921. Any returned man or the dependent of any returned man has to show up to that date, many months after he took off the King's uniform, that the disability, no matter how slight, the aggravation, no matter how slight, is pensionable, not only for himself, but for all his dependents.
Now let me come to the point which my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) brings up. I quite understand his point, which is this. He says that the onus of proof should not be on the returned man; that it should be entirely either on the country, the Pension board, or whoever acts for the country.

I will read the amendment just in a moment. According to this, what has any returned man making a claim for pension to prove? He has to prove any illness, not necessarily an illness caused by a gunshot wound, not necessarily an illness which he might have suffered while he was overseas, but any illness at all which was incurred on service. If he has been damaged by reason of that illness incurred on service, even an ordinary illness which he might have had at home, he is pensionable, and if he dies as a result of that illness, his dependents are pensionable also.
Every man in the army has a medical history sheet. It is true that when men joined up in the army, their medical history sheets were not made out in the most careful manner; but while they were in the army, their medical history sheets were kept in a fairly accurate manner, and everything that occurred while a man was on service was entered on that medical history sheet. That is reasonable and proper proof as to the state of the man's health during his service. Then he left
the service. Some men were discharged on what is known as the short form. The short form simply discharged the man as fit. The long form gave a history of the man's condition at discharge. When a man reported on discharge that he was not physically fit, the long form was used, and that obviated many difficulties. But many men reported on the short form, and it is of those that I wish to speak at the present time. When a man was discharged out of the army on the short form as fit, he may have become sick one year, two years, three years after the 31st August, 1921, the date of the declaration of peace, and his record during the war, his medical history sheet may or may not have been clean. If he becomes sick years after the *>yar, he is pensionable provided that there is the slightest connection between his illness and the illness which occurred while he was on service. Mark this; this is not a question of a military illness, not a question of a wound which he might have received; but if he had a natural, ordinary illness on service and later on after discharge, notwithstanding the fact that he was discharged with a clean record, if there is any connection set up in any way between the last illness I speak of and the first illness, he is pensionable. That has been the practice.

many such cases in Montreal, which is no exception. There were such cases all over the Dominion, and some of my military friends in the House will probably confirm that statement. These men were taken on and to all intents and purposes they were perfectly well.	As soon as they left a

But I do claim that under the act as now drafted, under section 11 and under the other clauses providing for courts of review and a federal board of appeal, the ex-service men are given every possible opportunity to prove their cases. Some hon. members may say-I do not say it myself-that at the present time these men perhaps are not getting what they should get. I think myself that as a matter of fact the Board of Pension Commissioners, except in isolated cases, do pension men to the best of their ability. But even if the men do not always get a fair hearing, you have boards of appeal. The act is so drawn that every man has an opportunity to show any reasonable connection between the disability from Which he is suffering and the fact of his having enlisted. Is not that fair enough? Or are we going to take an amendment of this description, not knowing what it will entail?

Mr. Chairman, a year ago when the minister's estimates were up I recommended that a commission should be appointed to inquire into the hundreds of vexatious cases that had arisen in the last few years in regard to the treatment of our returned men by the pension commissioners. My suggestion perhaps went a little further than what the minister proposes to-night, but I congratulate him on having appointed a royal commission, I congratulate the commission on the very able report they have submitted to the minister, and I am very glad indeed that he has introduced this bill. I have read it over carefully, and while there are other sections in the act in which many of
us could suggest changes, I believe, taking it on the whole, that this bill is most commendable and meets a long-felt need. I am sure all of us could detail many cases that have come to our personal knowledge in which we consider that grave injustice has been dealt out to our returned men. I might instance one case which is probably typical of dozens. The man went overseas, served his country, developed pneumonia, was in hospital, came out before he should-which was probably his own fault-insisted on going back to service, and remained at the front to the end of the war. During the demobilization, as we all know, the feeling on the part of every officer, non-commissioned officer and man in the Canadian Expeditionary Force was to get out of the army and back to civil life as quickly as possible, and to accomplish this they exercised their ingenuity to the fullest extent to secure their discharge papers and left the service as class A men, whereas if they had been medically examined they would not have been so classified. The particular man whose case I am dealing with got back to his job without delay. A year later he developed tubercular trouble and is now in the Hamilton sanitarium. His medical history sheet discloses that he had pneumonia overseas and that he passed out of the army Class A; but the doctor at the sanitarium, an expert on tuberculosis, says that the man's trouble was caused through service at the front. That man has not been paid one cent by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment since he has been in hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is a clear case for appeal.

It is Captain Nicholson's case. I wrote three letters myself, but his case was turned down. As I understand it now, that man's case can be appealed and reviewed' and if he can substantiate by expert medical evidence that his tubercular trouble is attributable to service he will be entitled to compensation.
The only suggestion I would make is in regard to section 11, subsection (a). I think probably the word "reasonably" might go ahead of the word "attributable," so as to make the line read, "was reasonably attributable to or was incurred during such military service."
Probably I am the one principally responsible^ for the record office for the Department of National Defence. I took a great deal of trouble in connection with its establishment. I remember very distinctly bringing a recommendation before Council in the early stages of the war, for as minister I felt that nothing
Pension Act

should be omitted by the government, or the Militia department, to ensure a proper record being preserved of the service of every officer, non-commissioned officer and man belonging to the Canadian Expeditionary Force. I took this course advisedly, having some knowledge of the fictitious claims made against the American government after the Civil War. I felt it was incumbent upon the government or the minister in charge that the country should be protected against unreasonable claims, and although I am not taking any credit for it; the credit belongs to the departmental officials -I believe that our records are the most perfect of any preserved by the belligerent countries. Those records are so complete that to-day our doctors scrutinize them when tubercular and other troubles develop after returned men have gone back to civil life, although as a matter of fact I believe the trouble is reasonably attributable to service. I congratulate the minister and shall be glad to support his bill.

I rise to ask a question, not of you, Mr. Chairman, nor of the minister, but of the members of this committee. Before doing so I must give the setting. For nearly a whole year we have had a commission of very able men dealing with the subject now under discussion, and they have submitted an elaborate and evidently carefully thought-out report-a report which singularly enough appears to have been received with satisfaction by everybody concerned, and more particularly by the returned men. We have the further fact of the hon. minister in charge of this bill coming before this House making this statement-and I have heard it at least half a dozen times-that it was his intention to bring down legislation carrying out the full intent of the report of this royal commission. He now tells us that he is doing so, that he has studied the act very carefully-and he has shown us to-night that he has a grasp of the subject which I am sure no one else possesses-and that he has had the very ablest draftsmen frame these amendments, and he tells us further that he has submitted these amendments to the people who after all are most vitally concerned-the soldiers themselves-and to the Ralston commission, all of whom have signified their approval.
The question I now ask the committee is this: Can we, sitting here to-night, expect to obtain such a grasp of the subject as would enable us to amend or improve the work of the royal commission, of the minister and of the draftsman? I think if we attempt to do anything of the kind we shall only add con-
[Mr. Mewbum.l
fusion, and that we had better accept the amendments in the form in which they have been submitted to us and see how they work out for a year. If this were the work of the Pension commission I would say: Let us scrutinize it down to the last syllable and the last comma, because I do not think we are satisfied with their interpretation of the act. But under the circumstances outlined I think we might do well to pass these amendments of the minister more or less in their entirety.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to a suggestion along the same lines as that indicated by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). All members have received, I have no doubt, and certainly the members from Toronto, the statement issued the day before yesterday by the Great War Veterans' Association, and I would ask that it be made a part of the record of this debate, so that we can say that not only has the royal commission reported what they think is in the interest of the men, but that the men themselves, the members of the Great War Veterans' Association, endorse the report This is the communication, Mr. Chairman: Ottawa, June 13, 1923.
Re Pensions Appeal Procedure
Sir,-I am instructed by the Legislative Committee of the Dominion Veterans' Alliance to solicit your support of legislation designed to establish the form of pensions appeal procedure recommended by the Royal Commission on Pensions and Re-establishment. The principal features of the procedure so recommended are set forth in Sections 9-13 of the Bill proposing certain amendments to the Pension Act which is now before the House of Commons.
I may explain that in each province, evidence and suggestions, relative to this subject, were placed before the royal commission by a committee representative of all groups of ex-service men. Great care was exercised by these committees in weighing all ideas discussed and in advancing those most practicable under conditions prevailing in respective provinces. It is believed that the recommendation of the royal commission on this matter embodies the principles generally regarded by ex-service men as fundamental in any provision for appeal. It is also believed that the form of appeal procedure recommended will achieve the maximum of satisfaction with a minimum of expense.
Experience gained in dealing with the grievances of individual ex-service men before and during the inquiry of the royal commission has led this organization to the conclusion that thousands desire to appeal from decisions of the Pensions Board. This experience has also resulted in the conviction that the procedure outlined by the royal commission offers advantages vastly superior to any plan yet proposed. This procedure ensures justice with economy and invites confidence. It may not be amiss, therefore, at this juncture to point out some of these advantages.
The procedure recommended enables a discussion preliminary to appeal which will tend to eliminate appeals without legal ground or, of a frivolous character and those caused by obvious errors. In this way, without undue restraint upon the appellant, the work and expense of the appeal administration may be materially lightened.

Pension Act
The constitution of the appeal boards as recommended by the royal commission ensures a common-sense treatment of the appeal, free from professional bias and undue emphasis upon technicalities. Members with legal and medical experience can most readily deal with legal or medical aspects of the claim, and the presence of a member with industrial experience will provide a viewpoint most essential in estimating the degree of incapacity as gauged by the requirements of the labour market. It is also most essential that members of every board should have knowledge of conditions which prevailed on active service.
To avoid dissatisfaction, it is desirable that the large number of appeals awaiting consideration at the outset, should be reviewed with all possible speed. The hearing of each appeal will necessitate a careful examination of the appellant's service record a proceeding which, with the present system of records, requires a great deal of time, even by those with experience. The procedure recommended will provide a personnel available and competent to engage in a review of all appeals lodged, without undue delay and continuously while necessary.
The proposed district review boards are easily accessible to the prospective appellants either from the standpoint of location or time. If at the outset this work were entrusted to officials unable to engage therein without interruption, many men in certain occupations would find it difficult to appear during the appeal proceedings. Furthermore, it is presumed that the district review boards will arrange hearings in various centres in the district as may be convenient.
While the procedure recommended is designed to adequately cope with the initial deluge of appeals, nevertheless, it offers the most certain assurance of ultimate economy in administration. The administrative machinery may be telescoped as the volume of appeals may diminish. Provision is made for a gradual centralization based upon the federal appeal board which would not be possible under any other scheme proposed.
One of the foremost advantages of the proposed legislation is that uniformity with regard to decisions and procedure in the various districts is definitely safeguarded. The required reference to the Pensions Board and possibly at a later stage the Federal Appeal Board, provides a balancing and harmonizing influence. There is little danger, as the work progresses, of any variation of decision at different points upon appeals based upon similar evidence. Under any lack of the other schemes of district appeal procedure proposed lack of uniformity would be inevitable. Another advantageous feature of the appeal legislation in view is that federal supervision may be exercised over all decisions as regards expenditure of federal funds.
I trust that these views \nay receive your favourable consideration and support.
Yours faithfully,
C. G. MacNeil,
Secretary, Dominion Veterans' Alliance.
Here we have the Dominion Veterans' Alliance endorsing this scheme. I agree with the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) that we ought to be very careful about disturbing this very well thought-out plan as so endorsed.

Mr. Chairman, as a past member of the Pension committee of this House for three years I wish to corroborate some of the statements made by the minister to-night. I desire first, however, to congratulate him on the bill which he has 246
introduced. So far as it is possible to remedy by legislation the disabilities under which the returned man has been suffering, I think his bill will achieve that end. However, I want to go just a little further than any hon. members have gone whom I have heard speak to-night. I did not have the advantage of being in the House when this matter was discussed on Monday evening. I am speaking now of the interpretation of the act. I think it will be practically impossible to pass a pension act that will be so administered by the present Pension board as to get justice for the returned man. Hon. members may not all agree with me in that, but I feel sure that a good many of them will. I want to cite a special case to prove my contention, a case which in my opinion is fully covered by the act, but in connection with which justice has not been done, and I doubt if it ever will be done while the present chairman of the Pension board holds that office. He has always taken the attitude that once he makes a decision he must not reverse it for fear he will be admitting he had done wrong.
Oh, I object to that.
I take exception to my hon. friend's attitude in that respect.
I have the floor.
I simply want to register my objection.

I want to cite this case so that the facts may be understood. This man enlisted within ten days after war broke out, went to France, and came back discharged as no longer fit for service. He was one of the men referred to by some hon. members here to-night as those who were anxious to get back to civil life. He was over military age when he enlisted; he served two years and then broke down under the strain. He had three sons of military age who enlisted and were in training while he was overseas; they went to England on the same vessel that brought the father home. He was therefore very anxious to get back to his family-a wife and three small children. As I say, he was discharged as no longer fit for military service, not even as A-l. He tried to carry on in civil life, but he broke down within a month and went under the doctor's care. He made the mistake of not going to a military hospital and undergoing examination by military doctors. He employed a civilian doctor, and by the way, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment paid that doctor's bill afterwards-I presented it-to the extent of $100. After carrying on



Pension Act
for upwards of two years under conditions such as these, trying to work, breaking down and going under the doctor's care-not entering a military hospital but undergoing treatment by his own practitioner-his condition at last compelled him to go to a military hospital. He was sent to a sanitarium in St.
John, New Brunswick, which is
10 p.m. under the direction of a very competent man, Dr. Farris by name. After being under Dr. Farris' care for a matter of three months he was granted full disability pension for tuberculosis; I hold in my hand a copy of the communication notifying the man that he had been granted that pension. But after that pension had been paid for two months it was discontinued. The case had been reviewed by a medical man here in Ottawa who had never been within five hundred miles of the pensioner, who had two months before been granted a full disability pension. His pension was cut down to $5.30 a month, which was supposed to be in respect to a gunshot wound in his knee-and that pension was for himself and his wife and three children. I at once got in touch with Dr. Farris, whom I know very well, and whose ability and honesty have never been questioned. I asked him what he knew of this man's case. I knew the man personally. I knew he was a hardy robust man before he enlisted; that he had returned from the front broken in health and that he has since been unable to do a day's work, or, if he has done it, should not have done it. I would like to read the following letter from Dr. Farris dated April 6, 1920:
Dear Sir,-Driver James B. Tompkins, No. 5216, 1st Field Co., C.E. C.E.F., was a patient in this institution for several months. I believe he had pulmonary tuberculosis. He went out of here in good condition with the disease quiescent. I examined him again in the fall of 1919 and thought he was not so well and recommended his return to this institution. I was surprised to learn that h.is pension had been cut off and the Pension board did not believe he had tuberculosis. He had had pleurisy and bronchitis before d scharge and he had a hemorrhage about a year after his discharge. On March 10th, 1920 he was admitted here again, as his wife said he was in a very bad condition. I was unable however to find any definite tuberculosis th:s time. His lungs had cleared up and his general condition was fair. I found his heart weak and I believe he has arteriosclerosis. I feel confident that this man had tuberculosis at the time of h:s discharge, that he made splendid improvement while in here, and that he has taken pretty good care of himself since, but-
This is what I want hon. members to notice particularly:
-that he is unable to do but a small amount of work, apparently due to arteriosclerosis and also to tuberculosis. He certainly should get more than $5.30 per month for his pension.
IMr. Caldwell.]
I also communicated with the doctor who attended him in his home after his discharge, and this is the letter I received from him.
Woodstock, N.B., December 28, 1920.
May say for your information that I attended this man first on July 10, 1916. I believe he was discharged from the army in June, 1916. The man had at that time a slight hemorrhage from the lungs I have attended this man ever since, and there is no doubt that this trouble was induced by active service. He was a strong, robust man before going to the front, and since that time his health is such that he is unable to earn a livelihood. He has spent several months in a sanitarium, but the trouble ds still present. This man without doubt should have been receiving a pension since this trouble started.
I have repeatedly taken this matter up with the Pension board, submitting these facts to them for their information. They did not have Dr. Farris' letter or either of Dr. Grant's letters at the time they discontinued the pension, and I was' fully convinced that upon receiving this information they would reverse their decision and reinstate the pension. But they persisted until last year in refusing anything more than the pension for gunshot wound that I have mentioned. Here is a letter from Dr. Grant dated March 3, 1922- and I may say this letter was unsolicited; Dr. Grant wrote me knowing that I was' interested in the case. He says:
Woodstock, N.B., March 3, 1922.
Mr. J. B. Tompkins is ill again and has had another hemorrhage from the lungs, his condition is certainly unsatisfactory so far as any improvement is concerned.
Dr. Grant at that time took the matter up with the Camp Hill hospital at Halifax with a view of having this man admitted for treatment, because he was in very poor financial circumstances and was unable to pay a doctor. The Pension board was unwilling to admit that he had a claim for pension. This was the reply Dr. Grant got from the Camp Hill Hospital in Halifax, dated March 16, 1922;
Dr. N. P. Grant,
Woodstock, N.B.
Your communication of the 10th inst. relative to the marginally noted man has been passed to this office.
You are advised, please, that B.P.C. Ottawa, have definitely ruled that this man's pulmonary condition is not to be regarded as due to service. No steps can therefore be taken to have him admitted to any S.C.R. institution.
They refused to admit him to a sanitarium even for treatment, although he and his- three sons had given splendid service. The three sons went over in 1916 and served during all the remainder of the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
He was ultimately admitted, was he not?

Pension Act

Yes. I will come to
that later. Dr. Grant forwarded a copy of this letter to me and I at once took the matter up with the D.S.C.R. here. After my insisting very strongly that action be taken they did admit him to a sanitarium for treatment, and upon my taking the matter up quite strenuously with the Pension board they granted him an increase in pension. Here is the letter from the Pension board dated July 28, 1922.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon.
gentleman is going beyond relevancy to the matter under consideration when he reads extensively from these let' ers.
I was not present when the principle of the bill was before the House the other night. However, I should like to be permitted to refer to these communications.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I question whether
that record can be read. A good deal of what has already been read has been irrelevant.

I will bow to your
ruling, but I would like to refer to it if I may not read it. On July 28, a communication was received from the Pension board saying that they had granted him a pension of $21 a month for himself, his wife, and three children. I think it is a 15 per cent disability that gives a pension of $21 a month, and they made this retroactive for the whole period from his discharge, after, for three years, refusing to give him anything but $5.30 a month and stating that his condition was not due to service. Then in July, 1922, they yielded a little and they admit that his condition is possibly due to service and they grant him a pension that I consider an insult to a man who has given the service that he has and who is not able to work as he is not. But due to the fact that he must live, he has gone out and worked repeatedly for a short time. Each time he breaks down and comes back on the doctor's hands. His wife, who is not a trained nurse at all, leaves the children with him when he is not able to work and she goes out and endeavours to get nursing in order to try and keep the wolf from the door. Their home is mortgaged, their taxes are not paid, they are in a very critical financial condition. The three sons who have returned have married and have had as hard a time as most returned men to reestablish themselves, and should not have to support the father and mother and the smaller children. However they have had to contribute from their very meagre earnings, after
246i
maintaining themselves, to the upkeep of the family. One of the sons bought a farm from the Soldier Settlement board, made his 10 per cent payment down, but owing to adverse conditions has lost that. So that this family that have given such great war services do not feel, nor do their friends feel, that they have at all had justice at the hands of the Pension board.
What pension does the man get now?

He is receiving a pension of $21 a month for himself, his wife and three small children Every doctor that examines him tells him that he should not work but he finds that he must do so. When he works a little he breaks down and comes back again on the doctor's hands. When he gets on his feet he endeavours to work again, but without success. These facts have repeatedly been brought to the attention of the Pension board. The letters I have quoted from have been referred to the board. I have taken the case up repeatedly with them. Their last stunt was to call in a tubercular expert to go over this man's file of papers. That was on May 29th, 1923. I have a letter from the board stating that the medical expert, after reviewing the man's file-here in Ottawa whereas the man lives in Woodstock, N.B.-had decided he was not entitled to a pension.
Now to substantiate the statement which has already been made by some members, and which may still be repeated by others, I may state that I think the present Pension board have made their position untenable by the attitude they have taken towards the Pension Act and towards pensioners. For instance in the case of the amendments of 1920, and 1921, questions were asked by various members of the parliamentary pension committee who wished to assure themselves that those amendments would not affect the men of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. Had the members of that committee-I think I can speak for myself anyway and I believe the same remark applies to other members of the committee-believed that those amendments would have been applied to the men who served in France, or in any other theatre of war, they would not have been passed. But the Pension board, or their representatives, said those amendments did not apply to the Canadian Expeditionary Force, but simnly to the men in the permanent force, and applied to conditions after the war was over. It was stated without hesitation that the amendments would not apply to any man who had served in the overseas forces. Ac-
Pension Act

cordingly the amendments were allowed to go through. For that I think we are all to blame. I think a separate clause should have been framed to deal with the permanent force leaving section 11 as it was. However, I am pleased that the minister has brought down section 11 in its amended form.
I now wish to quote from the report of the Ralston commission to substantiate the claim that the Pension board have not given the pensioner the benefit of the doubt in a great many cases. On page 114 the report of the commission reads as follows:
Sufficient <haa been shown, in the evidence before the commission, to quite justify the concflusion that the statement that the applicant is given the benefit of any reasonable doubt cannot be taken as expressing by any means an invariable principle of pensions administration. Numerous cases were presented in which, in the opinion of the commission, there was clearly a reasonable doubt established in favour of the applicant, but pension was refused; and in many of these the appflicant showed not only a reasonable doubt but a preponderance of evidence in his favour.
This is the finding of the royal commission after having had submitted to them, I think I am safe in saying, hundreds of cases in which the pensioner was not given the benefit of reasonable doubt. I do not wish to weary the House by quoting copiously from the report but in many places it is stated that statements derogatory to the pensioner were taken at their face value while facts established in his favour were not considered. That is to say, that facts operating adversely, against the pensioner were given very great prominence in the matter of deciding on pensions. I can personally vouch that I have found this to be the case. Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to weary the House but I must say I feel very strongly on this matter. As a member of the Pension committee of this House for three years I have had as good an opportunity to know the attitude of the Board of Pension Commissioners towards the pensioners and towards any change in the Pension Act that would be for the benefit of the pensioners as any hon. member in this House.

I rise to speak only
because I wish to emphasize and make a little more clear, if I can, the necessity, as I believe it, of giving in a case of doubt, the decision in favour of an applicant for pension. I think the minister did not quite understand the purport of the amendment when it was proposed. No one desires to lay violent hands on this section 3-a long section with many subsections and, if I may be permitted to say it, well drafted-but I want to put this case to the minister: Suppose
fMr. Caldwell.]
there is an applicant who is suffering from a disease which if attributable to or incurred during military service would entitle him to a pension. Suppose we have one suffering from such a disease who goes before the Board of Pension Commissioners. There are two doctors who say, "Your disease is attributable to the war or to your military service." There are two doctors on the other side who say flatly "Your disease is not attributable to your military service." In other words, suppose, as very often happens, it is a case of fifty-fifty, that there is no preponderance of testimony in favour of the plaintiff, that the verdict can only be the Scotch verdict, "not proven." Now, what is the position of the Pension commissioners? I do not know whether they are sworn to administer their duties faithfully or whether they take an oath of office. No doubt they do do that whether they take such an oath or not. They are in this position then, "We cannot award a pension. The case is evenly balanced. We cannot say this is attributable to the war, nor can we say it is attributable to military service. Therefore it is impossible for us, under this admirably drawn act, to award a pension." What I desire is that when the case is on an even balance the onus of proof shall favour the applicant, and that the even balance shall be immediately disturbed by saying that the applicant is entitled to his pension. The British House of Commons has done that; the government introduced an act. I believe it was in 1922 or 1923. We are told we have the best Pension Act of any country that went through the war but we do not have it in this respect. We may have been liberal with those entitled to pensions, but that is not the only consideration. I would like the minister to tell this House if it is possible under this admirably drawn act, for the Board of Pension Commissioners, discharging their duties faithfully according to the oath of office, if they take it, where the evidence is evenly balanced, to decide in favour of the applicant and grant a pension. I submit it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course the Pension
board may decide in favour of any applicant, if there is a difference of opinion between two medical boards. There is nothing at all in the act that would preclude a decision in favour of an applicant, if two medical men pronounce against the attributability and two pronounce in favour of it.

I am afraid I have not made myself clear. The members of the Board of Pension Commissioners must discharge their duties honestly. Instead of tak-

Pension Act
ing two doctors for and two doctors against,
I	will take one doctor for and one against. The applicant comes before the board and makes his claim under section 3, subsection
II	(a), and one surgeon says "Your disease is not attributable to nor was it incurred during military service." The other surgeon, equally credible, comes forward and says "Your disease is attributable to or was incurred during military service." What is the board to do? The board may say that either of these two distinguished surgeons is entitled to credibility, but that "We cannot believe A any more than we can believe B; it is an even balance, the onus of proof is upon the applicant, and therefore we have to deny the pension". Of course, as the minister says, there is nothing to prevent the board from granting a pension, but if the board is discharging its obligations as men sitting in judgment, it is impossible under the law to give a pension to the applicant.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I beg to differ with my
hon. friend. There is nothing whatever in the act that precludes the board from awarding a pension in the case he has cited. My hon. friend is speaking of attributability, but we go further than that in this act. We say that if it is attributable to service the man may be pensioned and shall be pensioned-not "may" but "shall"-also if the disease was incurred during service. It is absolutely impossible to go further, and if you attempt to go further you confuse matters entirely. I admit that very often one medical opinion is set against another medical opinion. Medicine is not a science of geometry nor of mathematics, and doctors disagree. How can we expect that they will not disagree, when lawyers disagree on a given statute? When the Pension board refuses a pension in a case such as my hon. friend mentioned, the remedy would be to appeal. I do not know whether my hon. friend is a lawyer by profession or not.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Then, as a lawyer he
knows that contradictory evidence is submitted in the court in almost every case. It is a matter for the judge to estimate the evidence of one party as against the evidence of the other party. In numberless cases the evidence is contradictory, and if the litigant loses his case before one court it is open to him to appeal to a higher court; if he is not satisfied with the second court, he may go to a third court, or he may go as far as the Privy Council.

Although it appears to
me that I have laboured hard I have not made myself plain to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes, the hon. member has made himself very clear.

The minister must admit there are many cases where the evidence is evenly balanced. The applicant has just as much in his favour as the defendant has in his favour; in other words, there are cases where there is no preponderance of evidence, you are in a dilemma as to where the right may be, and you would seek to have some additional evidence in order to decide the case. But it is not forthcoming. In that case the board has no option and no alternative but to refuse the pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
On what does the hon.
member base that assertion? Will he quote me one single line in the act that precludes the awarding the pension?

I will read the section.
Such a provision does exist in the English Act. I am sorry now to take up the time of the House, but I must do it. The section of the act reads:
In respect of military service rendered during the war-
(a) Pensions shall be awarded to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability resulting from injury or disease-
Let me skip a few words here.
When the disability resulting from injury or disease or the aggravation thereof in respect of which the application for pension is made or the injury or disease or the aggravation thereof resulting in the death in respect of which the application for pension is made-
Then what?
-was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
Suppose a man qualifies under the first-part of the section I have read, and come? as an applicant for a pension, what must he show? He must show that this disability,, disease or the aggravation thereof was attributable to or was incurred during such military service. Suppose he produces evidence, as I have said before, and that ranks fifty in authority, and there is evidence against that which amounts to fifty; there is an even balance, and that man, under the act of the hon. minister, must be denied his pension, if the Pension board does its duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
All I can say is that I beg to disagree with my hon. friend. I ask him to quote one single sentence in this act that would preclude the awarding of a pension in such a case under this act. He cannot show one single sentence. Of course, there is no
Pension Act

such preclusion in the act, and my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, knows it. It is a question I understand of appreciation of medical evidence as presented. It is not a quest'on of one doctor as against another. I would not set my medical opinion against the opinion of a professor of pathology in McGill University or Queen's University, though it might be one medical opinion as against
not her medical opinion. It is for a competent board to judge the situation, to appreciate the evidence as presented, and to award or refuse a pension according to their judgment and their conscience. There is in the act nothing that precludes them from awarding a pension, even if the evidence is not adduced.
Does the applicant have to prove that his disease was attributable to his military service?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or incurred during military service?
Or incurred during military service?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is different.

I was stating just one case. It is very plain that if you can prove that your disease was attributable to military service, you get a pension. I will put the matter in this way. Does the minister admit that an applicant must prove that his disease was attributable to or was incurred during such military service?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not say that he has to, and there is in the act nothing that says that.
What does the language mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The language means that he may make application for a pension for a disability which is attributable to or incurred during service.
He must show that.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: He may and, no doubt, he does show all possible evidence that is in his possession. It is for the Pension board then -and they do this in every case-to resort to securing medical opinion from their advisers in this regard, from the medical sheet, from whatever is produced by the man, and to base their judgment thereupon.

I think possibly I may
offer just one suggestion that may help to clear up the point. Probably the hon. member

for Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) is correct as to the legal letter of the law, but at the same time it would be an absolute impossibility in many cases for men applying for pensions to prove that their disease or disability was due to or was incurred during service. Take the case, for example, of a man who became ill a year after his discharge. He was discharged as fit. His case is laid before the medical board who finally say: "Well, the evidence looks as if this might have occurred at that time." Unless there is some medical record, it would be impossible for that man to prove in a legal sense, that his case was due to or was incurred, during service.
He has to do that now.
I do not think so. The argument I was making the other day was that you cannot live up to the letter of the law, as the Pension board has been inclined in the past to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: That is my impression also.
I hope this amended act will put an end to this living up to the letter of the law.

The last few lines of paragraph (b) of clause 3 read:
Provided that no pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which at such time was wilfully concealed, was obvious, was not of a nature to cause rejection from service, or was a congenital defect.
As regards a man who had a congenital eye condition, if it was proven that his condition was aggravated by service, would he be denied a pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No. He would not be pensioned for the pre-existing disability, but he w'ould be pensioned for the aggravation in this case. If that was not a congenital defect, or if it was not wilfully concealed, or if it was not obvious, then he would receive a pension, not only for the aggravation, but for the preexisting disability if he reached an actual theatre of war. That is the purpose of paragraph (b).

In reference to this discussion about proving a case, I would suggest that there is practically no such thing as a man proving his case. A man may prove his case, in the event of an application on account of some obvious disability, by the evidence of his comrades who saw it occur. But that happens only in a certain number of cases. As regards many diseases, such as medical diseases, these things are not proved. I do not suppose the minister would suggest for a moment that these cases are subject to proof.

Pension Act
What then is the question? It is a matter of a man submitting his case to the Pension board. If a man submits a reasonable amount of evidence, then his case is established; but one does not mention that in the same breath as proof. The case is not proved to a mathematical demonstration, but it is accepted on the establishment of a reasonable case. I think we are a little liable to confuse these terms in that sense.
As far as I can gather from reading the amendment, it conflicts with the latter portion of paragraph (b). That may not be the case, but I consider this amendment is of such a length that it should be printed and circulated amongst the members. Personally I do not feel able to discuss it until I have had a fair opportunity of reading it over very carefully. Many very serious difficulties have arisen in connection with pensions over the fact of obscurity and difficulty in interpretation. I fear we have expected too much of the Pension board in that respect, because they have had great difficulty from the act just as have returned men and others who are interested. We should be most careful to see that we make this act now as amended as perfect as possible. Especially we should gain from the experience we have had in the last few years of difficulties that have arisen through imperfectly and obscurely drafted acts. This amendment is too lengthy to be read over in this way unless we have an opportunity of reading it carefully as we have had of reading the bill. I, therefore, would suggest that if the amendment is to be proceeded with, it be allowed to stand for this evening until printed copies can be distributed amongst the members.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The four last lines of paragraph (b) to which my hon. friend (Mr. Mac-Laren) has referred are a repetition of the act of 1919 and have remained in the act ever since. They are not new.
The minister misunderstood me. I am referring to the amendment proposed to the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The amendment now before the committee?	[DOT]
My remarks are not on the amendment, but on the amendment to the amendment.
As I understand the matter, the insurance principle was contained in the 1919 act. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We called it so.
Then in the 1920 amendment, that was wiped out?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.
Is it not a fact that since the act was amended in 1920, pensions have actually been awarded to ex-members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force on the insurance principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: If that is a question, I shall answer it.

I was going to give, perhaps, a concrete illustration of that. For instance, if a man who had suffered during service from a light form of tuberculosis, let us say, had been cured and had gone back to service, and subsequently to his discharge, say in 1921, he again developed tuberculosis and applied for a pension, is it not a fact that a pension would be granted in such a case where the medical history of the man showed that he had suffered from the trouble on service.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think so.
In other words, although the act was amended in 1920, the insurance principle has been carried out during subsequent years?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I pointed out a minute ago that the due to service principle did not appear to have been applied until 1921. My hon. friend perhaps has not in mind that the declaration of peace took place only on the 31st of August, 1921, although the act had been amended more than a year previously.

I was not thinking of that, but of cases that arise to-day, cases of tuberculosis, or any other disease, the origin of which can be found in a man's medical history sheet. What I am suggesting is that a pension will be granted even to-day as the law now stands. Is not that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I think it happens, yes.
Well, as I understand the matter, these amendments which are now before the committee are simply for the purpose of crystallizing the practice which is now in existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.
I cannot get any meaning from the minister's answer, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Though in some cases pensions might have been awarded on the insurance principle, in at least 500 cases, I am informed by the Pension board, pension has been refused on that very account, because
Pension Act

under the act as it stands to-day, the disability in respect of which the application is made may not be attributable to service, even though it might have been incurred on service.

I agree with the amendment to that extent, in so far as it corrects that feature. I want to emphasize what the member for East. Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) said. I agree with his interpretation of this amended bill. True, we may be looking at it from a legal standpoint; we must take that into consideration. But suppose you have a case in which there are say, two doctors, on either side. The case comes before the Pension board and we find that after a perusal of the opinion given by the doctors in the first instance, the two medical men on the Pension board absolutely agree with two of them against the man, so that there is an adverse decision. It is very dangerous for the man's case if there is equal evidence on both sides, and even if the two doctors on the Pension board disagree, the situation is serious. So long as it is necessary for the man to show that his disability is attributable to service or was incurred on service there is going to be dissatisfaction, and there are going to be difficulties. It is my desire to see this dissatisfaction obviated and these difficulties overcome as far as possible this present year. I believe that this, section will be of service to some extent, but you cannot get away from the fact that evidence must be produced that the disability is attributable to service. After a period of two or three years there will be considerable difficulty in satisfactorily proving this, and there must be differences of opinion where there are medical men. Furthermore, I can quite understand that applicants for pensions will be firmly convinced that their disabilities are attributable to service, or were incurred on service, and these men will be able to obtain independent medical opinion supporting their view, though you may find medical opinion produced by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment unanimously opposed to it. There will always be differences of opinion among medical men, and that is going to give rise to difficulties and dissatisfaction. The minister says that this is where the appeal board comes in. That may help to some extent, but even the appeal board will be faced with the problems presented by the member for East Toronto, and I am not satisfied that this section is going to meet a very large number of cases which are bound to be appealed as soon as the appeal boards are constituted if the sub-
sequent sections are adopted. In my experience, these sections simply crystallize what has been the practice of the Pension board. I have had no particular difficulty in cases which I have presented to them where I could show that disability was attributable to service. Where I could do that I have had no particular difficulty in having the insurance principle applied. Yet I quite understand that there have been cases all over Canada, some 500 in number, which have arisen where that principle has not been applied. In that regard I agree with the amendment, because that principle, I think, should be applied. I submit, however, that we are not getting over the whole dissatisfaction, which is bound to result when the bulk of these appeals come before the board.

Whilst I agree to a large extent with my hon. friend from Toronto and the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Clark) that something should be done to take the onus of proof as to the attribu-tability of the disease off the applicant, I think the amendment offered by the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) opens the door altogether too wide. Let me give an extreme hypothetical case. A man, let us suppose, was called to the colours and drafted in 1918. He reported to the barracks and was given harvest furlough. He was probably ten minutes at the barracks when he was given furlough, and he went home to his farm. Before he reported back again the armistice was declared. Thirty or forty years afterwards he develops tuberculosis. Under the amendment, the fact that he reported to the barracks, was medically examined and passed as fit, is conclusive evidence that he must have contracted tuberculosis on service and he would be entitled to a pension. I think hon. members of the committee will agree that that is opening the door a little too wide and would certainly lead to a considerable abuse. As I have already stated,
I agree with the other legal lights that at present the onus of proof is on the applicant, and something should be done to open the door a little wider in this respect, but I think we are going a little too far under the amendment offered by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner).

Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that as we have been discussing this amendment for a little over two hours, and as probably all opinions in regard to it have been elicited, we might as well decide one way or the other and get on with this bill.

Pension Act

The amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) deals with the definition of the word "attributability", which I think he desires to incorporate in the act. The amendment now before the committee goes a great deal further. I do not think it is advisable to define the word "attributability", I think any definition will only tend to narrow its meaning. But if it is desired to define "attributability" in such a way that the onus will not be entirely on the soldier, let us make an amendment along that line.

A year ago, Mr. Chairman, I might not have supported this amendment, but to-day, after my experience in the interval, I am inclined to support it. The onus of proof at the present is too difficult for the applicant to sustain. Let me remind the minister of one case which illustrates this very strongly and will convince him that something must be done to alleviate the applicant's burden. I brought to the notice of the department the case of a man who after having a pension for four years finds himself suddenly deprived of it because the Pension board discover they made a mistake. What mistake did they make? Referring to their records, they find it reported that there is a scar on the left side of this man's neck which was there before the war. The man denies this and states that after he was discharged he went over to Glasgow and there had a slight operation performed, of which this scar is the mark. The board refuses to accept his statement or to take any steps to prove or disprove it. As a result the man has to go to the trouble of sending over to Glasgow to get some person there, who is not interested in his case, to go through the hospital records. What are the facts? This man had a slight operation performed in Scotland in 1910-he worked from 1910 to 1914 in the shipyards there-then became a fireman on a convoy, worked right up to 1914 in perfect health-served a year or more on the convoy-jumped his job at Montreal- went to Belleville and enlisted-and a month later showed signs of tuberculosis. That is a very unfortunate case, but it is not the only one I have brought to the department's notice. I find it is very difficult for the applicant to bear all the burden of proof, and yet there is nothing in these amendments to relieve him of that burden in any way.
Last year I supported the amendment that time should not count with a tubercular case. The man perhaps had been under a gas attack with no immediate bad effects. I think tubercular cases should be in a class by themselves. Neurasthenic cases should also be sympathetically considered if the men can prove they suffered shell shock while actually at the front. There are one or two of these amendments that appeal strongly to me, and if the minister is prepared to relieve an applicant of the full burden of proof I shall support them.

Mr. Chairman, may I
change the amendment in the fifth line? I should have put after the word "who" these words: "having served in a theatre of actual war."
The error arose owing to the English act being differently worded.

Mr. Chairman, I protest vigorously against an amendment like this being read into one of the most complicated acts on our statute books. I believe that not half a dozen men in the House can read the amendment correctly into the act, and for myself I decline to take the responsibility of dealing with an amendment of this description without having it put before the law officers of the Crown for their consideration.
Mr. LeSUEUR: From the discussion so far it appears that a number of members feel that this section puts upon the applicant the onus of proof. That, of course, is the ordinary legal principle in all courts, and one would naturally expect it to be the case here. 1 understand that the minister's interpretation of this section is that the matter is entirely in the discretion of the Pension board.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. LeSUEUR: To make it absolutely clear I have been wondering if it would be satisfactory to him to insert before the word "attributable" the words "was in the opinion of the board reasonably attributable." That might possibly cover any question of doubt in regard to the onus of proof.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no objection to the words being inserted.

Before the clause carries, I would ask for a definition cl the words "wilfully concealed" in the fifteentn line in subsection (b). There was a period of enlistment when the greatest care was not exercised by the medical examiners in passing volunteers, and many men were accepted without being thoroughly examined. A large number of men were so anxious to enlist that although they may have suffered from such a disability as flat feet or poor eyesight, which afterwards developed into a serious condition, they did not disclose it at the lime for fear they would be rejected. Who is to determine when a man wilfully concealed any disability?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that the board has experienced any difficulty at all, certainly since I have been minister I have not heard of a single complaint in this regard. "Wilfully concealed" I think would mean, for example, the case of a man who on enlistment failed to mention that three of his toes were missing, and after discharge, because of having served in a theatre of actual war, claimed a pension for the loss of those toes. Well then, the board would say, "You lost them before the war?" and if the answer was in the affirmative, the board would say, "You wilfully concealed that when you enlisted." I do not think this restriction has caused any difficulty. The words "wilfully concealed" were in the original act of 1919: they were in section 25 (3) of the act of 1920; they were in the legislation of 1921 and 1922. If there has been wilful concealment and a man is confronted with that provision of the act, he admits it immediately and there is no further difficulty.
Mr. LeSUEUR: Before the committee proceeds with clause 4 I would like to crave the indulgence of the minister and of the committee to propose an amendment to the interpretation clause, subsection (b) of section 2, in which the words "widowed mother" are, to some extent, defined.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend referring to the Pension Act?
Mr. LeSUEUR: Yes. Under section 47 of the Pension Act, supplementary pension is given to the widowed mother, wife or children of persons domiciled and resident in Canada at the outbreak of war who enlisted in the military forces and who died in service or as the
[The Chairman.]
result of service. Last year the House in its wisdom defined the words "widowed mother" as extending to and including a mother deserted by her husband. I wish to propose an amendment to the interpretation clause, comprising the addition of the following words:
And also a mother whose husband is in a helpless and dependent condition.
Possibly I can best explain what I believe to be the justice of that amendment by citing a case. A boy who had been the support to a certain extent of his mother and a rather sickly father-the father was unable to work continuously-enlisted in the Royal Air Force. He went to the front, fell within the German lines and was killed. The father later became paralyzed; today he is a helpless paralytic, who has to be fed by the mother of this boy and given close attention. The result is that simply because her husband is living, though in a helpless condition, she is unable to collect any supplementary pension in respect of her son's death. From a monetary standpoint she is in a much worse position than if the husband had died; if her husband were dead she would be clearly entitled under the act to collect pension. As it is, she has to give her time to the nursing of her husband; it is a drag on her resources to maintain him, and solely on account of the peculiar wording of the act she is prevented from obtaining a pension. My amendment is to cover cases of that kind.
I rise to a point of order. I submit that the amendment just proposed is out of order in that it involves additional expenditure on the part of the Crown.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I may say that the resolution which preceded this bill provided in part as follows:
That enactments be made respecting pensions for military servics rendered during the war and after the war, which shall be made retroactive to the first day of September, 1919, and all cases in which pension has been refused, reduced, discontinued or underrated by reason of the fact that the proposed legislation was not included in the Pension Act shall be subject to review by the Board of Pension Commissioners-
And so on. There is no limitation in the resolution which prefaced this legislation as to the amount of public expenditure that 11 p.m. is to be involved. As to the question of a private member not having the right to move an amendment in committee which would increase the public expenditure I may quote the following from May, page 461:
This principle, however, is apparently disregarded when the recommendation of the Crown is given to a resolution empowering the expenditure of public money which, framed in general terms, places no limitation on

Pension Act
the amount of expenditure to be authorized by the resolution. As the resolution sanctions, without any specific limitation, the application of money to be provided by parliament to certain purposes, when the clauses in a bill founded upon such a resolution are before the committee, the freedom of action sanctioned by that resolution can be exercised.
So I must rule that the hon. member's point of order is not well taken.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to discuss the matter at length but I would call your attention to decisions rendered on a similar matter four years in succession when amendments to the Pension Act were brought down. On those occasions I proposed that a certain extension be applied to the words "widowed mother" in the act, and that widowed mothers be granted additional pensions. On every occasion my amendment was ruled out of order by the then chairman of committees, the present member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin). I think these decisions should form some kind of jurisprudence; at least, they ought to be looked into before the Chairman gives a definite decision on the point of order raised now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have made some inquiry into that, and I am informed that in those instances the resolutions in each case dealt specifically with each particular part of the subject matter of the bill; they were not only very definite in that respect but they were very explicit as to the exact extent to which the bill and the powers and rights created by it went. I understand that the resolution which prefaced the introduction of this money bill was prepared in the widest terms so that the minister would be in a position to consider any amendment that might be offered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the amendment, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment is that there be added to the interpretation clause the words:
And also a mother whose husband is in a helpless and dependent condition.
The question is upon the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The purpose of the amendment is to consider as a widowed mother a mother who is not a widow but whose husband is in a helpless condition and utterly unable not only to earn his own living but also to care for himself. There is in the Pension Act as it exists to-day, in clause 34, subsection 3, the following provisions:
When a parent or person in the place of a parent who was not wholly or to a substantial extent maintained by the member of the forces at the time of his death subsequently falls into a dependent condition such parent or person may be awarded a pension provided he or she is incapacitated by mental or physical infirmity from earning a livelihood, and provided also that in the opinion o<f the commission such member of the forces would have wholly or to a substantial extent maintained such parent or person had he not died.
I believe the case referred to by my hon. friend would be covered by section 34, subsection 3 of the existing law. I do not think his case would be improved by adding as he proposes to the interpretation the expresison "widowed mother." I have no serious objection to accepting the amendment of my hon. friend. It will have very little consequence financially and I realize the force of the point my hon. friend has made, as to the position of the widowed mother under the circumstances he has mentioned. As far as I am concerned I do not see anything that would be unjust in the proposition of my hon. friend. I even believe it would be fair and generous. I would suggest, however, that my hon. friend read clause 34, subsection 3, carefully and see if he does not think that the case in question is covered by that particular subsection.

I appreciate the remarks of the minister as to the fairness of the proposal but section 34-3, as I read it, refers to a member of the Canadian forces. This amendment is proposed to cover the case of a member of the royal forces and refers to the supplementary pension to a widowed mother, and would come under section 47 of the Pension Act.

speechtext:
I am afraid in that case
the point of order raised should be seriously considered. At any rate we might perhaps wait for a few seconds until my hon. friend has thoroughly considered the effect of the subsection which I quoted.

I am satisfied on that
point.

which the minister refers and it does not seem to me that it would cover the case represented by my hon. friend. Anyhow since the minister admits that the amendment would meet the case and would only involve a very small expenditure, why not accept it and let us pass on?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
