Before you pass to the next clause there is a matter I would like to bring up but I do not know whether it would be appropriate to do so at this stage or not. I should like to ask the
Pension Act

minister a question with reference to the time of the appearance of disability. In the case of a widow an amendment was passed by this House last year to the following effect:
(1) Pensions shall, in all cases, be paid to tihe widow of a member of the forces without reference to the time of appearance of the disability, which resulted in his death, unless and until it is substantiated that the marriage of such member was contracted with the intention of procuring pension for such widow, and not a bona fide carrying out of the agreement, provided that such disability shall not have been caused by the act of such member or through vice, and that pension be only payable while such widow remains unmarried.
I believe that amendment was rejected by the Senate. What I should like to ask the minister is, whether it is at all possible for him to see his way clear to reintroducing some clause that would cover that particular point. There was a case in the city of Winnipeg, perhaps the minister may recall it, of Lieutenant Phinney, that very well illustrates the unjustness of the present arrangement if I might just mention that case in a few words. Lieutenant Phinney died as the result of a disability incurred upon active service, and within the meaning of the Pension Act, incurred prior to the time of his marriage. He enlisted with the Fort Garry Horse in August 1914, but in an effort to reach France . he transferred to the Imperial Forces. He was taken sick and returned to Canada and discharged in March 1916. His health recovered and he again volunteered in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and was given a commission in the Canadian Field Artillery. He proceeded overseas and went to France in October, 1917. In February 1918, he was gassed and evacuated to England where he remained in hospital for some time. He made a complete recovery and was discharged A1 for active service in May 1918. Prior to returning to France he was married in England. He served with distinction until the conclusion of the war. winning the Military Cross for his splendid daring and skill in bringing his battery into action in front of the infantry lines at the battle of Cambrai. Upon discharge he was in receipt of a pension, but upon his demise the widow was refused pension on the grounds that the marriage had taken place subsequent to the appearance of the disability. His marriage was contracted at least six months prior to the armistice. The Board of Pension Commissioners admit that death was attributable to service. There has never been any question of "fortune hunting" in this case but because of the inclusion of this unjust provision in the act pension is denied the widow of this splendid soldier.
I Mr. Woodsworth.]
I have no amendment to offer but it seems to me that the amendment of last year probably covers the ground. If not is there any other way in which the minister could meet the situation.
Where can we find the text of that amendment?
This is an amendment, I believe, which was introduced last year.
I cannot find it any place,

It is possible I have the amendment here that is referred to. I could not follow the wording as given by the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) but it appears as section 5 of the amendments of last year. By the way, this is one that had been suggested by myself before the Pension committee during three successive years; it was defeated by a very small majority for two years but last year it carried in committee, was recommended to the House in the report of the committee, was passed by the House, but was rejected by the Senate. The amendment reads as follows:
Subsection one of section thirty-three of the said act, as amended by chapter sixty-two of the statutes of 1920, is further amended by inserting after the words "married to him" in the second line thereof the words "within one year after date of discharge from the forces or".
That covers, I believe, a very limited number of cases. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) when he says there is very great hardship in some of these cases. For instance, a member of the forces who enlisted and went overseas but was not married, contracted a disability due to his service and came back and married afterwards and his widow gets no pension if he dies of his war disability. There is another clause in the Pension Act-and I am sorry I have not got a copy of the act before me-which provides that a pension may be granted to a wife if a man lived with her before he went overseas even if not married to her. I think the comparison is odious, and I do not like to make it, but I think, in the case of the man who married even within one year of his discharge or of the appearance of his disability, that his widow should be entitled to the same pension as if he had been married before going overseas. There was an objection raised to it in the first year, and the first amendment I moved two years ago was that if he was married within five years of his discharge, or after the appearance of his disability, the widow would get a pension. The next year

I would hate to attribute such a motive to any one. I strongly urge the minister to make this amendment to this bill. I think the number cf cases was quite limited. I do not remember the exact number, but it was given to us. On section 11

Appeals to district review board:

I move that the following words be added at the end of subclause (1):
Which recommendation, if favourable to the application for pension, shall be final and shall be adopted by the Board of Pension Commissioners.
In support of that, I may say that I see no reason for sending this application for pensions from pillar to post. The Pension board deals with it. Its decision is adverse. Then you have the district review board, and I submit that the opinion of the district review board, if favourable to the applicant, should end the matter. There is no reason why the government and the public should desire to set aside the decision of the district board, if that decision is favourable to the applicant. Such a decision, I think, should be regarded as final.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I am unable to accept the amendment. My hon. friend will see later, as we proceed, that no alteration of the district board's decision can be made by the federal appeal board unless the appellant who received the favourable decision is given an opportunity of appearing personally before the federal board. I think that is a guarantee that the whole scheme will work with some uniformity.

Has the minister considered how many appeals are likely to come to the federal appeal board under subsection 3? The federal appeal board must review substantially every case that goes before the district board.

They will have as many cases as are decided upon by the district appeal boards, with the exception of those appeals, decided by the district boards, which

Pension Act
are carried into effect by the Board of Pension Commissioners.

There is an appeal from the decision of the district appeal boards. In other words, if a soldier appeals to the district appeal board and that board says his case was not properly treated by the Board of Pension Commissioners, the commissioners can appeal to the federal appeal board, if they want to.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They may refuse to carry out the recommendation of the district appeal board, and if they do so, automatically the appellant's case goes to the federal appeal board.
That is not the way the bill reads.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It is. Let me read the provisions for my hon. friend. They are as follows:
(4) In oases where the recommendation of the district review board is more favourable to the applicant than the decision appealed against, the federal appeal board may not disapprove the recommendation without giving the applicant an opportunity to appear personally, or be represented before it, at a hearing in the district in which the applicant resides, or at the seat of the federal appeal board as may be deemed more convenient. On this hearing, the federal appeal board shall make such final decision as may appear just.
The section my hon. friend refers to is this:
(2) In case a recommendation more favourable to the applicant than the decision appealed against is not carried into effect within a time specified by regulations made under the powers hereinafter con' ferred, or in case of a recommendation not more favourable to the applicant than the decision appealed against, the recommendation and fyle containing all papers in regard to the case shall be forthwith transmitted by the Board of Pension Commisioners to the federal appeal board, and the Board of Pension Commissioners may at the same time submit for the information of the federal appeal' board a statement of their reasons for not carrying into effect the recommendations of the district review board.
So that if the Board of Pension Commissioners should refuse to carry out the decision of the district appeal board in, say, Halifax, they will have to transmit the decision of the district board in Halifax to the federal appeal board, with a statement of their reason for not carrying it into effect, "and the decision of the federal board shall be final.

It is my opinion, which I offer for what it is worth, that section 11 constitutes exceedingly cumbersome and expensive machinery for the country to carry out. It means that every single decision, good, bad or indifferent, can be appealed from. I do not believe that the federal board will be able to function owing to the enormous number of cases which are likely to come be-

fore it, and in addition to that it is my opinion that the soldiers themselves will find the procedure unsatisfactory. I do not want to go into the matter in any great detail, because one could say very much about it; but this is not the system which has been adopted after a great deal of experience in England. There the practice is that the soldier may appeal on a question of entitlement, that is to say, as to whether or not his injury or aggravation is attributable to war service, which immediately brings him under the act. But on a question of assessment, unless it is the final assessment-and there are final assessments there that is where a soldier is given a certain pension for a definite period-the soldier has an appeal to the boards constituted under the department. In my opinion, I repeat, this is expensive and cumbersome machinery, and I doubt whether the federal board will be able to function. The district review boards will be encumbered with an enormous amount of work, and I do not think that the federal appeal board will be able to deal with all the cases that will be submitted to it, nor do I think that the soldiers will be any more satisfied than they are to-day.

I think we are all committed, first, to the unit appeal boards, and also to the federal appeal board. My hon. friend (Mr. Marler) has made a deep study of the question and he is sincere in the views he advances. But I am not concerned at present as to whether this procedure is either cumbersome or expensive. I hold the view that if it is in the interests of the returned soldiers of Canada it should be made effective. As the minister has pointed out, if the district appeal board's decision is not carried out by the commissioners, there is a further appeal to the federal board; automatically, on the refusal of the board of commisioners to carry out the district board's finding, the matter is taken to the federal board. That is only in keeping with the principle that underlies our courts of law. We have various courts of law that are both cumbersome and costly; nevertheless, they are very effective. I believe that the gentleman who framed the report of the Ralston commission, and who is a sound lawyer, saw the point of view of the British people in affording every opportunity of appeal to the returned soldiers.
This is not the British system of appeal in these cases.

I am not saying that it is the British system in regard to pensions, but it is undoubtedly the British principle of juris-

Pension Act
prudence. The principle embodied in the provisions of this bill follow that principle as closely as possible.
Follow what?
The system of British and Canadian jurisprudence.
It does not follow the British system of pensions.

I have already stated that the system proposed in connection with these appeals is not the British system in regard to pensions. What I am pointing out is that it is consistent with British principles of jurisprudence. It provides an appeal step by step to a tribunal which will be ultimately binding. With regard to the amendment of my hon. friend from Yukon (Mr. Black), I know that that hon. gentleman is absolutely sincere in his regard for the welfare of the returned soldiers of Canada. The hon. gentleman's amendment, however, might work very disastrously to the cause of the returned soldiers.
No.
Well, let us consider the matter. Does the hon. member desire to make the district appeal board's decision final?
If favourable to the applicant.

Then I do not think that is quite fair. The applicant, of course, is a returned soldier, and while I desire to see everything given the returned man that we can possibly give him, at the same time we must administer British law impartially both to the applicant and to the other party interested in the matter. There must not be one law for the applicant and another law for the Board of Pension Commissioners. If you have a court of appeal it must be open to all who are interested in the questions it has to decide; and if you have a district appeal board and you declare that a decision which it makes that is unfavourable to the returned soldier shall be appealed against, but that any decision in the returned man's favour shall be final and be subject to no appeal, then you are obviously creating class legislation in this country, which personally I do not like. I emphasize once again the fact that I am as favourable towards giving to the returned soldiers all that we can possibly give them as is any other member in this House, but I do say that we must treat all alike. I agree with my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Mar-ler) that the section will be rather cumbersome and perhaps somewhat expensive. But
I do not regard this as any insuperable objection to it, for I certainly think it will safeguard the rights, both of the returned soldiers, whom we all want to see protected, and of the exchequer of Canada. I am therefore thoroughly in favour of the provision.

I want to say just a few words in regard to subsection 2 of section 10 with reference to tenure of office. It has been pointed out that the commissioners shall be appointed for a period of five years. There are three of them, two at $6,000, and one at $7,000, or, in all, $19,000; and over the period of five years this will mean a total expenditure of $95,000. We are therefore tying ourselves up for this amount for salaries alone, and the minister knows very well that in addition to this there will be secretariats of various kinds, besides travelling and other expenses. Instead of making these appointments for five years, I would suggest that we make them for two. For this reason. Supposing at the end of a couple of years that this system was not found satisfactory, or that under it practically all appeals had been dealt with, and that consequently it was desired by any government then in power to do away with this expensive civil service, under the present legislation they could do nothing, whereas if we made the appointments for two years they could be renewed from time to time while the necessity for the board continued. I know the argument will be advanced that it would be difficult to get men to serve for two years, but I do not think so. I fear that we are building up not only in this branch but in all other branches a civil service which is an appalling expense to the country, and I think the time has come when we should take seriously into account the large salaries of these executives. I think, without interfering with the efficiency of the proposed board, we might very well cut down the tenure of office to two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was also my desire to have this federal appeal board appointed for as short a period as possible. I may point out that the Board of Pension Commissioners is appointed for ten years, and the salaries are exactly the same, $7,000 for the chairman and $6,000 for each of the commissioners. It is of course impossible to fix lower salaries for the federal appeal board commissioners than those we have granted to the Board of Pension Commissioners. Now, if we should reduce the appointment to two years I am afraid it would not be possible to find three outstanding men willing to give up their vocations and devote the whole of

Pension Act

their time to this work, because it is provided in one of the subsections of section 10 that these commissioners shall devote the whole of their time to the performance of their duties and shall not engage in any other occupation. That is my reason for thinking they should be appointed for five years. I asked the opinion of the members of the royal commission on this very question, and at first they suggested ten years, but on further consideration they thought five years would be more satisfactory. The members of the district review boards will be appointed for one year only and will be part time men, in view of the fact that after a year we expect there will be a great contraction of their work. It may be that by that time the number of appeals will have decreased so considerably that two or three district boards will be sufficient to deal with them. But I believe it will be the sentiment of parliament in the years to come that there should always be in Ottawa a federal appeal board above the Board of Pension Commissioners. To-day we are the only belligerent country in the world without an appeal board. I grant the expenditure will be large, but what we have to do is in discharge of what we consider to be a national duty to our returned men. I remember when the Land Settlement Act was introduced in this House by the previous government the measure contained so many provisions that appeared cumbersome and difficult of application that we doubted whether it would be a success. During the first year there is no question but what we will experience many difficulties under this measure, and whether we shall be able to overcome them entirely or not remains to be seen, but I hope we shall be able to rise superior to all of such difficulties.

In reference to the point raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), while there may be some question as to this measure being cumbersome, I was very much impressed to-night by the speech of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). He pointed out that for one year an able commission, presided over by a very capable soldier-lawyer in the person of Lieutenant-Colonel Ralston, had been travelling all over the Dominion investigating soldiers' grievances, and as a result of the evidence submitted to them they had made certain recommendations. They have made certain recommendations, and I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that we might fairly accept those recommendations. They come as the well-matured suggestions of those who have had 	:	glU
to do with questions of this kind, and I hardly think that we here to-night, who may not, perhaps, have had much experience in the matter, should suggest changes in the proposals made by the commission. In refer ence to the appointment of a district board the Ralston commission says:
After considering all the suggestions received from representatives of ex-service men and the systems in vogue in both Great Britain and the United States the commission has come to the conclusion that an appeal procedure which would meet conditions in Canada and fairly protect the interests of both the ex-service man and his dependents, and the country, would be the following which is hereby recommended:
(a) The establishment, under the Department of Justice, of a district review board for each of the nine D.S.C.R. districts, and of a federal appeal board for the Dominion of Canada, the personnel of each of these tribunals to consist of a medical man, a lawyer and a layman, at least two of whom shall be ex-service men.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that every Great War Veterans' organization in this country recommended that before the Ralston commission?

That makes their recommendation all the stronger. I think we may very well declare that part of the section carried. I suggest also that the recommendation of the Ralston commission in reference to subsection (c) be adopted, namely, that the time within which the entering of appeal may be made be one year instead of three months. On page 17 of their first interim report the Ralston commission say:
The right of appeal to be open for one year from the coming into force of the regulations, or for one year after the decision complained of, whichever may be last.
But in the bill the one year is changed to three months. I think that three months is entirely too short a time within which appeal may be entered, particularly having regard to the fact that our soldiers are scattered all over the face of the globe. I do not know why we should not adopt the recommendation of the Ralston commission and make the time one year. I beg to move that-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is already an amendment before the committee, moved by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt this amendment?

I think the minister's attitude in connection with this amendment is a correct one. He has very properly referred to the question of uniformity. You cannot have a final decision by one district board which may be entirely out of harmony with the final decision of a board somewhere else. An automatic appeal to the federal appeal

Pension Act
board secures uniformity throughout the whole Dominion. If you do not have uniformity you will have continual complaints from soldiers, because many of them will find out that in one part of Canada the soldiers get one sort of treatment, and in another part, another. So that an appeal to the federal appeal board is absolutely necessary.

The remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) would seem to indicate that the district appeal board is of no use whatever. Why have a district board at all if you are going to go on to a federal appeal board? Why not make your appeal direct from the Pension board to the federal appeal board? The district review board is of no use; it cannot give a decision that will be acted upon in any event. It is only an additional expense and an additional worry to the returned soldier. He will make application to the Pension board for pension; if the board rules against it the appeal goes to the district review board, and no matter what decision they give, there must be an appeal to the federal appeal board.
Not necessarily.

If the decision of the district review board is in favour of the applicant, why not make it final? The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll) undertook to show how the amendment could be embarrassing to the returned soldier; (here is nothing more impossible in the world. It would be most satisfactory to the returned soldier-in fact, too satisfactory. How anything could be too satisfactory to the returned soldier to suit this House I am at a loss to understand. Why keep him dangling between one board and another? If the Pension board says no and the district review board says yes, why not let it go at that; why worry the soldier by asking him to go to the federal appeal board? Is not the country satisfied, is not the returned soldier satisfied, if the district review board decides in his favour?

Then the hon. member is in favour of doing away alto-
12 m. gether with the federal appeal board?

Not if the decision is against the returned soldier. Give him another chance; let him go to the federal appeal board if the decision is against him. But if the decision is in his favour the public should not want to combat the decision. * I do not think the minister wants to do it; I do not think the taxpayer wants to do it. It is an imposition on the returned soldier to force him to go from that district board to the federal board if the decision of the district board is in his favour.

Is it not a fact that
if the district review board decides against the pensioner he does not then go before the federal appeal board?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: He does.

The point taken by the
hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) is very much stronger than anything I could have said. Suppose, for example, that in the district of Halifax, which comprises quite a large area, a man suffering from tubercular disease gets a decision from the unit appeal board which gives him a pension, and out in Calgary a man under exactly similar conditions gets a decision against him. There is no doubt that there would be dissension if that condition existed. The man in Calgary would say, "Well, the eastern man has got the best of us; he has a decision from his board that we are unable to get from ours." The method proposed is based on the same principle as that which applies in the case of our courts: we have a trial judge, we have the Supreme Courts of the various provinces, then we have appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. That is what I was trying to point out to my hon. friend from Montreal a few moments ago. There is one question, however, I would like to ask the minister: I think I heard him say a little while ago that these amendments as drafted had been presented to the federal command of the Great War Veterans' Association, who had expressed themselves as being in favour of them. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
As soon as the bill was
printed I sent a copy of it to the office to which my hon. friend refers. The only suggestion I received from them was that the time within which appeal should be made might be extended to one year. That is the suggestion the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) made. They also suggested something along the line referred to by my bon. friend from Winnipeg, with regard to marriage after the appearance of disability.

I do not think it could be suggested for a moment that if the
Great War Veterans' Association or any soldiers' organization were asked whether a decision of the district board favourable to the soldier should be final, they would not say yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
Of course they would say yes.
Pension Act

Sub-section 2 says:
In case a recommendation more favourable to the applicant-
And so on. Who is to say whether the decision is more favourable or not to the applicant, who is going to be the judge of
that?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: My hon. friend asks who is going to say that?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Any child could say it. If you have a 20 per cent disability and you appeal to have more and 30 per cent is granted, I think anybody can say it is more favourable. If you have no pension, and you appeal, and you are awarded a pension, I think it is more favourable, but if your appeal is not granted then the recommendation is not more favourable. My hon. friend has not given any thought to that.

I have given some thought to the matter. The hypothetical cases which the minister has cited are easy of discernment. If a man's disability is fixed at 20 per cent and it is increased to 30 per cent it is easy enough to see that it is more favourable. But if the district board gives a decision in the ambiguous way in which the Pension board has time and again given it, and which no one not even a lawyer can interpret, it is going to be very difficult to say whether it is more favourable or unfavourable.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No such decision can be rendered.

They may have given a decision which in the end does not grant a pension but still it may be argued that it is more favourable than the decision retidered by the Pension board, and who is to say whether it is more favourable or unfavourable? I want the wording to be such as will make the decision of the district board final and let it go at that, that is if we desire to ameliorate the condition of the returned soldier.

I think a very strong argument has been advanced by the hon. member for Yukon. I know that very often in the past there has been a complaint among the soldiers that in case o{ an examination by a local board as to pension the result was told to the applicant and then the report was sent into the Pension commissioners at Ottawa, and there was some cutting down of the decision. I think the minister will admit that on many occasions under this

clause there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction. Certainly it has appeared to me many times to be rather a strange thing that when a local board of whatever number of doctors, three I think usually, examine a case and, we will say, award a 40 per cent pension, that after they have sent in their report to the Pension board it has been cut down to 20 or 30 per cent. It has always appeared to me very strange that the Pension board should presume-because that is the proper word to use-to alter the decision of the three men who have examined the man. In the same way in the cases mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Black) there would be some questions asked. It is true that the law makes provision that the applicant may appear before an appeal board but if unsuccessful he would have to pay his own expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Not before the federal appeal board.
He would if he was unsuccessful.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Not if he was unsuccessful.
Then I have read the clause wrongly.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I will read the clause if my hon. friend will listen to me:
The expenses of the successful applicant in appearing before the district review board shall be paid on the scale now allowed applicants brought in for periodical medical examination, and the expenses of applicant or his representative in appearing before the federal appeal board shall, if the attendance of either be required by that board, also be paid on the same scale.
Yes. But there is the provision "if the attendance be required by that board." He may not be required by the board. They may decide without requiring the attendance.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Will my hon. friend bear with me for one more second?
Yes. Will the minister tell us what clause he is reading?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I am now going to read
sub-section 4 of section 11:
In cases where the recommendation of the district review board is more favourable to the applicant than the decision appealed against, the federal appeal board may not disapprove the recommendation without giving the applicant an opportunity to appear personally, or be represented before it, at a hearing in the district in which the applicant resides, or at the seat of the federal appeal board as may be deemed more convenient. On this hearing the federal appeal board shall make such final decision as may appear just.

Pension Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are considering subsection 1 of clause 11 to which an amendment has been moved by Mr. Black (Yukon). Is it the pleasure of the committee that the amendment be adopted?
Amendment negatived.

I just wish to go a little further in order to get the point cleared up. I do not think that the two clauses the minister has read are necessarily to be interpreted as he interprets them. I think they may be interpreted that way or they may be interpreted otherwise. To repeat what the minister read:
The expenses of the applicant or his representative in appearing before the federal appeal board shall, if the attendance of either be required by that board, also be paid on the same scale.
The other clause quoted by the minister says, they shall give him the opportunity of appearing. Suppose they do not require him to appear but he takes the opportunity of appearing? I think the clauses conflict.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They cannot reach a more favourable recommendation without giving him the opportunity to appear.
I would not say that the interpretation is absolutely as the minister makes it.

I should like to
ask the minister who is to decide when the recommendation is more favourable or otherwise under section 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Well the decision itself expresses the fact in plain language.
Who is to interpret it, the minister, the board, or the returned soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
No; the decision itself. If [DOT] the appeal of the man for an increased pension is not sustained he does not get a more favourable decision. If he gets an increase of pension he has a more favourable decision. Nothing could be clearer.
Subsection 2 agreed to.
On subsection 5-Time for appeals.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Logan has moved an amendment to subsection 5 to strike out the words "three months" and substitute the words "one year" in lieu thereof.

Is that in accordance
with the recommendation of the commission, and is it satisfactory to the organizations of ex-service men?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The royal commission
recommended one year. I consulted the Department of Justice and asked them what was the procedure in the law courts. They intimated to me that a month or thirty days was usually the time allowed for an appeal. I concluded that perhaps three months would be a reasonable delay, that is how that period oame to appear in this clause. The recommendation of the conclusion was for one year. I realize that three months is too short and I am willing to accept it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On subsection 10-Payment of expenses.

There should be another section here in order to tie up the appeals with the Pension Act. I bring that to the attention of the minister, as section 11-
All appeals under this section shall be tried and decided under the provisions of the Pension Act and amendments thereto.
It is in order to tie up the appeal board with the Pension Act itself.
It is tied up now.
No, I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We should have a little more explanation. I did not catch the purport of the amendment.
The purport of that amendment is that when these boards of appeal are established they shall look to the Pension Act and amendments thereto as the basis of their appeal in law.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Is that not implied?
No.
When we constituted the Supreme Court I do not think we said, "All decisions shall be made according to the law."

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I would think it was implied.

The House can take it or leave it as it thinks proper, but I have gone through the section with the greatest care with those who understand the subject, and they tell me that they approve of my suggestion.
This is an amendment to the Pension Act, and all appeals and all trials under the amendment must be in conformity with the Pension Act.

If any amendment is to be made to the Pension Act no such clause as
Pension Act

this should be added. If it is necessary, of course I have no objection to it, but I do not think it is necessary.

In my humble opinion this amendment of my hon. friend, with all due respect, is ridiculous. You might as well put at the end of every act we pass a provision that the court shall adjudicate according to this act. It is the law, and they have to adjudicate according to it.

I am inclined to think the amendment is going to destroy all the good this present bill would accomplish, and that it will tie up the Pension Act in such a way that it will not function. I take it that it is nothing more than an amendment put forward by the sympathizers of the Board of Pension Commissioners.

The hon. member has no right to make that allegation, and I ask him very kindly to withdraw it. I can give him my word there is no such suggestion. I have studied the matter with great care, and I am just as much in favour of the returned man as he is. Perhaps he has not the discernment to see ic. This is a fair and open amendment. I do not force my opinion on the hon. member. I suggest that he withdraw the allegation he made.

I do not see that there is anything in the allegation to take exception to. The amendment presented is absolutely unnecessary. Many hon. members of this House and people outside of this House have studied this particular act. We had a commission that sat for a year for the purpose of suggesting legislation which would have no restrictions to prevent it from functioning. Each member of this committee sitting here to-night is just as eager to have legislation brought in that will function properly as are those members who are submitting the different amendments. As far as the allegations go, I cannot see that there has been any reflection, but it is a well known fact-and the opinion has been expressed in this House- that the Board of Pension Commissioners have not functioned as the people of Canada think they should function; and that is why this particular legislation is introduced. Therefore, I cannot see how I can support the amendment. _
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the title carry?

Before the bill is reported, I have an amendment which the min-
ister asked me to withhold until the other provisions of the bill were passed. It will be an amendment to section 33 of the Pension Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Section IS of the bill.

The amendment is-
Subsection 1 of section 33 of the said act as amended by chapter 62 of the statutes of 1920 is further amended by inserting after the words "married to him" in the second line thereof the words "within one year from the date of discharge from the forces".

I rise to pretty nearly the same point of order, as the last one. This amendment involves additional expense to the Crown. It is true in your decision, Mr. Chairman, you stated the minister had given notice and had brought down a resolution which was in very wide and general terms and could cover all possible amendments, but I will call your attention to the resolution. It says:
Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Pension Act, chapter 43 of the statutes of 19X9 and the amending acts, and to provide-
1. That enactments be made respecting pensions for military services-
The amendment proposed by my hon. friend for Victoria and Carleton is not respecting pensions for military service. It is respecting pensions granted in respect of military service.
I am surprised at the hon. member.

The widow of the soldier does not get any pension for her military service; so that under the strict interpretation of the wording of the resolution the amendment of my hon. friend is out of order. The widow gets a pension on account of the military service of her late husband, but she does not get any pension for military service.
Is that not true of all soldiers' widows who do get pensions?
Yes, it is true.
I think nobody but a lawyer would think of such a technical interpretation.
When a man has been caught up on these technical points so often, he does not see why somebody else should not suffer, particularly when he is pleading a bad case.

I am glad he admits the bad case.

Pension Act
I submit under the terms of the resolution the amendment is not in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I fear I must rule against the hon. member. The resolution preliminary to the bill, section 1, says:
That enactment be made respecting pensions for military services rendered during the war and after the war.
It does not say to whom these pensions shall be paid for the services rendered by those who did render such services, and pensions are payable to either dependents of those who might be classed as dependents. I think, in view of the discussion which has taken place, and in view of what the hon. member knows as to whom pensions are payable, that it must mean any person the House may decide is entitled to a pension.

All through the Pension Act we find these words, "pensions shall bs awarded to 1 or in respect of members of the force." When they say "in respect of members of the force" they mean to dependents on account of the services of members of the force. So that if the minister, when he brought down his resolution, wished to allow the field to be open for amendments which would grant pensions to other than those who actually earned the pensions on the field of battle, he would have said "for military service" or "in respect of military service." I submit that is the wording of the act; it is carried all through the act, and it has been carried through the act since 1919.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I feel I must find that the wording is more general and wider in the act than in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Caldwell).

What is the effect of the
amendment?

The effect will be to
grant a pension to the widow of a soldier who marries after his disability has appeared, if he was married within one year after his discharge.

Is this the same
amendment that was passed by this House a year ago?

Yes. After due investigation by the Pension committee last year, it was recommended in the report of the Pension committee that this should be embodied in the act, and it was passed by this House, I think without any dissent.
Yes, there was.

Possibly by the hon.
member for Quebec South (Mr. Power); but I do not think we took his suggestion seriously, even at that time, because he is very sympathetic to the soldier and his dependents. We all know that. When the bill went to the Senate, the bill was amended by cutting out this clause.

Whatever the hon. member
for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) may say, I have serious objection to this amendment, and I have objected to it even since I have been a member of the Pension committee, that is, since the session of 1918. I seriously and conscientiously believe there should be some finality about these pensions. The woman who marries an ex-soldier after the appearance of a disability, enters into this bond with her eyes open. She knows he is suffering from a disability, and she should not be pensionable at his death. If we now allow this widow to obtain a pension, I am morally certain that at the next election, -or if not at the next election, the election after that, because at the next election there will be a good government in power, but at the next election after that there might not be-we shall have this placed before the party which is in power: "You have already granted a pension to the woman who marries one year after the appearance of a disability. Why not extend that to five years?" The hon. member for Carleton told us at one time that he wished to extend it to five years. They might be asked: "Why not extend it to ten years? Why not extend it to the very moment before the death of the ex-soldier?" We shall have an ex-soldier at the age of seventy-five or eighty marrying a young woman and have pensions continuing in aeternum. We shall be paying more than they do in the United States, where they are paying more for pensions to-day than they were at the end of the Civil War. I am afraid to open the door. There are many cases which deserve sympathetic consideration; but if we once open the door, election after election we shall have to extend this and extend it until such time as we shall have a pension bill that the country will not be able to stand.
All kinds of promises were made at the last election.

Yes. The hon. member
made some, and so did I.
The pre-election promises of the hon. member for Quebec South seem to be haunting him somewhat.

No, they are not.
Pension Act

I have no fear of
pre-election promises because I made none. I do not feel that this is a radical thing to do at all. It was passed by this House last year without any serious dissent. It is a matter of justice due to the widow of a soldier, who married him within one year after his discharge. There is no danger of opening the door. Three years ago I moved this amendment in committee that it would be applicable to anyone married within five years of the discharge. At that time the five years had not elapsed, and there was an objection that this might be taken advantage of by some women wishing to marry a soldier for his pension. I did not feel there was danger of that then; but due to the fact that the year has expired some time ago, I do not think there is trouble to be feared in passing this amendment.

I feel that the door should be open to some extent to provide for a certain number of cases, and to provide for that certain number of cases, the door must be open for at least a year. There are a number of cases particularly of men who went overseas in the early stages of the war and who came back to the Old Country and got married. In that respect I fail to see how these particular widows can be provided for unless we open the door for at least a year. Although I am not in favour of going to any great extent, I should like to ask the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) in just what way he would provide for those that enlisted in the early stages of the war, went to France, returned to England and married, again returned to France and afterwards met with casualties, if we do not open the door for at least a year. Because those men enlisted in all good faith, went to France and back and were married, this all taking place before the Pension Act was drafted, before we had a Pension Act or any pension regulations. In that way I feel that this amendment is only meeting a situation that the country believes is fair and right.

I would simply not give
a pension to a woman who married after the appearance of a disability.
Does the hon. member not think such women are entitled to pensions?

No.
Amendment (Mr. Caldwell) agreed to: yeas 21; nays 17.

I beg to move:
That section 33, subsection (2) chapter 43, 1919, be amended by striking out the words:
"Provided that the death occurs within five years after the date of retirement or discharge of the date of commencement of pension."
I will explain this in a few words. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister the other evening and, while he did not express himself, I understood him to be unfavourable to the proposition. It is this. Suppose a man was wounded overseas and was 100 per cent disabled. He came back to Canada and his wife cared for him for a period of five years. He dies in the sixth year, and in order that his widow shall receive a pension she must prove that the man's death was strictly attributable to service. If she cannot prove this, the pension is not awarded. On the other hand, if the man dies within the five year limit, the widow is entitled to the pension. My contention is that if the man was so severely wounded as to come within any of the classes 1 to 5 the circumstances of his family are practically as bad as they would be had he been killed. In fact, viewing the matter apart from the question of his wife's affections, and considering, for the purposes of argument, merely the material aspect of the case, it would have been probably better had he been killed outright, because his wife must necessarily suffer considerably in supporting him. I think, therefore, that the time limit should be wiped out. I have in mind a particular case which I brought to the minister's attention and with which the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) is familiar. The case recently arose in that hon. gentleman's constituency of one Private MacPhail.
This man was absolutely blinded and was gassed, so that he was utterly unable to earn a cent in any way. He was a burden to his wife and died recently. Yet she cannot get a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The Pension Act provides that if a pensioner, who comes within the classes 1 to 5, that is to say. who receives a pension of 80 to 100 per cent, dies from any cause other than service before the expiration of five years, the widow will be pensionable just as though he had died from disabilities due to service. The provision was inserted in the Pension Act originally for the purpose of meeting the cases in the first few years of high disability pensioners. For instance, a man may have lost an arm or a leg or an eye. He would receive a disability pension which would entitle his widow, if he died within five years, to a pension, whatever

Pension Act
might be the cause of his death. That provision was made, I take it, for the purpose of affording the pensioner sufficient opportunity the more easily to support his disability. Since then the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act was passed by this parliament giving the privilege to any man in any physical condition whatever to secure insurance just for the asking and without medical examination. Such cases as my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) and my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) have mentioned would therefore come under the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. Any high disability pensioner could insure his life for $5,000 or less in favour of his wife and if any accident happened to him and he died of any other cause than disability due to war service his wife would receive the insurance. But in this case to which my hon. friend has referred, we must fix a time limit, and five years was considered reasonable. We hear of it now because the five years are up in some cases. Still it is the privilege at the present time of all those high disability pensioners to insure for $5,000 as a maximum. I submit that to the committee and am willing to abide by their decision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: What is the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark):
That section 33, subsection (2) chap. 43, 1919, be amended by striking out the words: "Provided that the death occurs within five years after the date of retirement or discharge or the date of commencement of pension."

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Do I understand it is the intention that for all time to come these men shall receive a pension, no matter what the cause of their disability is?	.

Not at all. Where a man is so severely wounded in the field that he becomes 100 per cent disabled, I want his case to be treated in the same way as if he had been killed. Because he is a 100 per cent disability case, therefore he is of no more value to his wife than the dead man would be to the widow.

It may seem almost amusing to talk in this way, but in the particular case referred to the man was 100 per cent incapacitated. He was blind, he had been gassed, and was absolutely a burden upon his wife.
There are many such cases.

It is apparent that in the case explained by the hon. member for Bur-rard (Mr. Clark) the wife might be placed in
a worse position than if her husband was killed, because if later he dies her pension is cut off, whereas if he had died at the front she would receive a pension. I think it is a very reasonable request and should be accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not think we are at present in a position to decide this definitely. I would propose to my hon. friend that instead of five years we say six, which will cover all the cases now pending.
It will not cover the very case cited by the leader of the Progressive party.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: When did this man die?
Just a few days ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: He will be covered.
No, he was discharged early in 1917.

This happened in the first year of the war when the man had only been overseas for a short time. He was taken prisoner by the Germans and through maltreatment he lost his sight. He came back in the early years of the war, and his case did more to enliven enlistment in the Brandon district than anything else that happened. It created that war spirit which proved such a stimulus to enlistment everywhere. But I can see the difficulty the minister has in mind.
Is this the case the hon. member brought up before the parliamentary committee last year?

No.
Amendment (Mr. Clark) agreed to. Yeas 25, nays 21.
Has the minister made any provision in the new legislation to take care of those Canadians who belonged to the British Expeditionary Force and do not get any pension at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: No.

I understand that some of those men get a small pension of $17, and are total disability cases. The pension is too small for their support. I think we might take care of such cases and make up the deficiency under our act.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: They have the option of taking the Canadian or the British rates.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion):
That there be added to subsection 2 of section 26 of the Pension Act 1919, and amendments thereto, the
Pension Act

following:	"Provided however, that the Board of
Pension Commissioners shall have discretion to pay the pension to any person who was being, or was entitled to be, supported by the pensioner at the time of his last examination."

This amendment is to cover such cases as I cited a couple of days ago. Suppose a man is being paid a 70 per cent pension, it is a temporary pension and he has to be examined every six months. Perhaps he gets into trouble or deserts his wife and children, goes across to the States and fails to reappear for examination. According to my understanding his pension is cut off. This amendment is to give the commission discretion to continue the pension to his wife and children as if the man had complied with the conditions. I think it is only just to the wife and children that this amendment should be accepted. There are not many such cases, but when they do occur great hardship results to the man's dependents. I do not think the minister could have any objection to this proposal, for discretion is left entirely to the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is a new principle entirely. A man may have died from any cause other than a war cause, and a pension would be awarded to the wife and children for three or four years after he died when in the ordinary course they would not be entitled to anything.

If after looking into the case the commission feel the man would have been allowed a pension, it would be entirely at their discretion to award a pension to his dependents. I do not think there are many cases which are left to the commission's discretion under this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There are a great many cases of desertion.

It would be up to the commission to decide whether the wife and children should be given a pension. However, I am in the hands of the committee.
Amendment (Mr. Manion) agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the bill?

Mr. Chairman, before the bill is reported I wish to again refer to a type of case which I mentioned the other evening and which I think should be provided for in this amended bill. The case is that of a man with a wife in Canada going overseas and contracting a bigamous marriage, although there were no suspicious circumstances and the second wife thought the marriage was bona fide. Subsequently the man was killed
[The Chairman.]
at the front and the widow in Canada claimed a pension. The act as it now stands requires that a pension shall be paid to one wife only. I made the proposal that under the circumstances I have outlined the pension should be payable to both women or at least that there should be a discretion in the Board of Pension Commissioners to so order. I put the facts of a particular case before the minister, and he stated that it could be dealt with without amendment. I wrote him to find out how, but I have not yet had a reply. Possibly he has not yet received my letter.
Did my hon. friend say that the man left two widows?
Yes.
Then one of them could not have been his widow.

Technically, that is so. But these are the facts: The man had a wife in Canada, went overseas, committed bigamy, but so far as the second woman was concerned she knew nothing about his previous marriage until after his death. She came to Canada, claimed a pension and was refused because the first wife made a similar claim, which was allowed.

But under the present act the commission may, in its discretion, give a pension to the unmarried wife. So I do not know what my hon. friend has to complain of. I think I remember two or three years ago a case similar to that cited by my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark). A man had been separated from his wife for seven or eight years, proceeded overseas, committed bigamy and later was killed in action. Both widows put in claims. The Board of Pension Commissioners, if my memory serves me right granted a pension to the unmarried wife on the ground that the first one had deserted him and was not entitled to any consideration. She had not written to him or had not lived with him for seven or eight years, therefore they thought the second wife was more attached to him, though she was not married to him-she could not have been, because he had already contracted marriage with another. For these reasons they gave her the pension. So that the Pension boar! has discretion to do the same thing in the case my hon. friend mentions.

The board has discretion, it is true, but here is a case where the wife who was left in Canada had a family and there had been no separation. The deceased, however, after going to France, had

Pension Act
married this other woman on the 29th of January, 1916, and he was killed on September 29th, 1916. A daughter was born of that bigamous marriage on January 4th, 1917. Both of these women are absolutely above suspicion, and consequently it was perfectly natural that the Pension board should award the real widow the pension. But it cannot be said that the woman who went through the form of marriage on the second occasion is not entitled to consideration. She contracted the marriage in good faith; her marriage certificate is produced and is above suspicion. [DOT]

After reflecting on the various phases of the Pension Act regarding the unmarried wife and cases such as the one mentioned by my hon. friend. I make this observation : that the boys are going to have a very good time in the next war.
